article_title: Waterford Upstart
citation: Waterford Upstart program description. (2024). https://www.waterford.org/upstart/
title: Short daily adaptive home-learning sessions sustained across the week
description: The program's usage pattern is short, frequent sessions: it "delivers daily 15–20 minute online lessons" and is "designed to be used consistently throughout the week," while the software "adjusts the level of support and difficulty as children demonstrate new skills." This combines brief session length, weekly regularity, and adaptive difficulty adjustment for young learners at home.
requirements: Daily access to a suitable device at home
Family support to maintain consistent weekly use
constraints: Session length and frequency as designed for PreK–2 children
target_learners: Children in PreK–2 learning at home
target_learning_goals: Early literacy, math, and science skill growth
examples: Daily 15–20 minute lessons in reading, math, and science used consistently throughout the week

article_title: Sharing Study Data: A Guide for Education Researchers
citation: Neild, R., Robinson, D., & Agufa, J. (2022). Sharing Study Data: A Guide for Education Researchers (NCEE 2022-004). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/pubs/NCEE2022004
title: Share study data openly to facilitate research transparency and accelerate knowledge development in education research
description: The guide's framing principle is open science: education researchers should make their study data available to other investigators rather than keeping datasets private. The guide states that "Open science envisions that researchers will make their study data available to other investigators to facilitate research transparency and accelerate the development of knowledge." The rest of the guide operationalizes this principle with practical decisions about what, how, and where to share.
requirements: Researchers must decide which study data to share, organize the data, and include documentation so other investigators can use the shared dataset
target_learners: education researchers preparing study datasets for sharing
examples: The guide walks researchers through deciding which study data to share, organizing the data, choosing documentation, and selecting a sharing venue

article_title: Temporal Network Analysis of Collaborative Prototyping from a Knowledge Creation Perspective
citation: Ohsaki, A., Tan, Y., Eagan, B., Shaffer, D. W., & Swiecki, Z. (2026). Temporal Network Analysis of Collaborative Prototyping from a Knowledge Creation Perspective. Journal of Learning Analytics, 13(1), 190–207. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2026.8959
title: Use short task durations to encourage sharing of incomplete ideas in knowledge creation activities
description: This principle recommends setting short time frames for collaborative activities to encourage learners to share incomplete and imperfect ideas rather than waiting for polished contributions. The article states "setting short time frames for activities to encourage sharing of incomplete ideas" as a design recommendation. The 30-minute session duration was chosen because it "could be embedded into typical 45- to 90-minute lessons in Japanese schools."
requirements: Tasks must be complex enough to incorporate all important design process activities despite short duration
constraints: Duration was selected for fit within Japanese school lesson structures; optimal duration beyond 30 minutes not tested
examples: Teams were given 30 minutes to design a wallet, which encouraged rapid sharing of imperfect ideas and iterative improvement

article_title: Parent Advisory Councils
citation: Building Better Parent Councils: A Research Brief. (2024). National Center for Families Learning. https://www.familieslearning.org
title: Set a shared vision with attainable goals and track progress to sustain council engagement
description: The brief recommends that parent councils orient their work around collectively developed aims tied to real school and community needs. It states that "Parent councils should set a clear shared vision and develop attainable goals that address key school and community issues, such as improving parent-teacher communication or advocating for student support programs." Tracking progress and celebrating successes are presented as practices that help sustain engagement.
requirements: A clear shared vision developed by the council
Attainable goals addressing key school and community issues
Progress tracking and celebration of successes
examples: The brief cites improving parent-teacher communication and advocating for student support programs as example council goals.

article_title: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding. (2016). Digital Promise, Accelerating Change. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Break instruction into short lessons with application, reflection, feedback, and encouragement when designing for adult basic learners
description: The brief's first design principle holds that the brain learns best in brief, focused bursts: short lessons let learners chunk information into meaningful units, then apply and reflect on each chunk to recall and connect it to later material. For adult basic learners this also connects to andragogy, since adults learn more effectively when new information links to their experience. The brief urges developers to build in feedback, checks for understanding, and encouragement around each short module.
requirements: Short lessons must be followed by focused activities that require learners to apply and reflect on what they learned
Feedback and checks for understanding should accompany each module
target_learning_goals: chunking new information with prior knowledge
deeper retention through application and reflection
examples: Cell-Ed developed ELL micro-modules consisting of a short audio lesson, a follow-up text reinforcing the lesson for learner reflection, and an interactive quiz for application

article_title: Shifting Education with Learning Pathways: Becoming Your Portrait of a Graduate
citation: Mills, K., Weisgrau, J., Burke, Q., Lee, K., Solorzano, T. and Coenraad, M. (2024, March). Shifting Education with Learning Pathways: Becoming Your Portrait of a Graduate. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/205
title: Shift from passive to active use of technology, using the Portrait to guide active integration
description: Drawing on the National Education Technology Plan's Digital Use Divide, the article recommends designing technology use so students engage in "active use" — "critical thinking, exploration, and creative expression" — rather than only skill-and-drill exercises and assessments, a passive pattern the article notes is more common for marginalized learners. It illustrates this with data practices: students may passively complete an online statistics module, or actively manipulate a data set to build a visualization presenting an argument to an audience, practicing the Portrait Skill Set of Communicating in All Media and Modalities while still computing the same descriptive values.
requirements: A Portrait framework identifying Skill Sets such as Communicating in All Media and Modalities to anchor what active use means
constraints: The article frames this as a promising framework rather than a tested intervention
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly those experiencing marginalization
target_learning_goals: Active, creative technology use including data practices
examples: The article contrasts an online statistical-analysis module with learners manipulating a data set to argue for a relevant issue to an audience

article_title: Developing a Feedback Taxonomy for Math: A Synergy of Perspectives through Data Mining Methods
citation: Seiyon M. Lee, Sami Baral, Hongming Chip Li, Li Cheng, Shan Zhang, Carly S. Thorp, Jennifer St. John, Tamisha Thompson, Neil Heffernan, Anthony F. Botelho. (2025). Developing Feedback Taxonomy for Math: A Synergy of Perspectives through Data Mining Methods. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 17, No 2. https://osf.io/puhyr/?view_only=514d8534e9be41d9a57ad82e9efb3249
title: Use an empirically grounded feedback taxonomy as a shared language when designing scalable feedback systems
description: This principle holds that systems generating or supporting feedback — human or AI-driven — should be organized around a taxonomy grounded in authentic classroom practice and co-developed by researchers and practitioners. The article argues that when integrated into learning systems, the taxonomy can support feedback that is "not only pedagogically meaningful but also more consistent, thereby reducing the variability often associated with human-authored feedback at scale." It further recommends using the identified types to guide LLM-based feedback generation and evaluation.
requirements: Taxonomy categories must be grounded in empirical analysis of authentic feedback data rather than derived solely from theory
Coding and framework development should include both researchers and practitioners as coders to account for varying interpretations
constraints: The article notes existing automated systems "often lack frameworks grounded in human-in-the-loop design principles, which limits their interpretability and pedagogical relevance"
The taxonomy was developed only for middle school mathematics teacher feedback
target_learners: K-12 mathematics students receiving feedback through digital learning platforms
target_learning_goals: delivering timely, pedagogically grounded, and consistent feedback on open-ended student work at scale
examples: The article states the identified feedback types "may be used to guide prompt engineering, fine-tuning objectives, or evaluation criteria" for LLM-based feedback systems.

article_title: Design and Implementation of the ESSA Resource Allocation Review: Lessons Learned in Utah
citation: Taylor, T., & Bowman, A. (2024). Design and Implementation of the ESSA Resource Allocation Review: Lessons Learned in Utah. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://web.stanford.edu/~mshanks/MichaelShanks/files/509554.pdf
title: Establish a shared vision among educational leaders that equal does not mean equitable before designing resource allocation processes.
description: The report's second lesson holds that because individuals bring different lived experiences to resource equity work, states should build a shared vision establishing that "equal does not mean equitable." This mindset shift, spread across the SEA and the state, is described as necessary to develop a process that identifies equitable resource allocation methods addressing student needs and expanding student access to educational opportunities.
requirements: SEAs must empower educational leaders across the entire system with the equity mindset shift.
target_learning_goals: understanding equity versus equality in resource allocation
examples: Recommended tips include conducting a gap analysis of leaders' understanding of equitable resource allocation, providing ongoing equity-mindset training and technical assistance, and designing the process as an ongoing exercise in equity rather than compliance.

article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Participate in Collaborative Discussions
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Participate in Collaborative Discussions. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://csaa.wested.org/resource/introduction-to-the-extended-thinking-through-discourse-continuum/
title: Shared regulation and co-regulation are social modes of regulation that emerge when students jointly construct knowledge
description: Drawing on Bailey and Heritage, the brief describes social modes of regulation in interactive learning environments: "group members regulate their collective learning (shared regulation) and students support the regulation of others (co-regulation)." Shared regulation means students collaborate to meet learning goals through projects, discussions, and other engagement — intentional interaction focused on goals, not engagement for its own sake. Co-regulation leverages peers to share knowledge, analyze each other's words and work, and give feedback; in classrooms prioritizing it, greater collective efficacy often arises among students.
requirements: Interaction with peers to move learning forward; intentional student interaction focused on achieving learning goals.
target_learners: English learners and their non-EL classmates
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated and collective progress toward lesson learning goals
examples: Peer feedback is described as the formative assessment practice that supports co-regulation, involving both individual reflection and collaborative discussion.

article_title: Social, Emotional, and Academic Development through an Equity Lens
citation: Duchesneau, N. (2020). Social, Emotional, and Academic Development Through an Equity Lens (#ReEnvisionSEL). The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/resource/social-emotional-and-academic-development-through-an-equity-lens/
title: Shift SEL focus from fixing kids to addressing adult beliefs, mindsets, and systemic policies that create learning environments
description: This principle calls for school and district leaders to approach social, emotional, and academic development through an equity lens by shifting focus away from "fixing kids" and toward addressing adult beliefs and mindsets and school/district policies that create the learning environment. The report argues "approaches that fail to acknowledge the influence of the learning environment, or fail to address the processes and structures in schools that disadvantage some students, may do more harm than good." It requires considering societal realities, individual realities, and cultural background.
requirements: Educators must examine their own biases and deficit thinking about students of color
constraints: Telling students of color to believe in their ability will not be effective if adults harbor deficit thinking and haven't addressed their own negative biases
examples: The report cites Chicago Public Schools training educators in restorative justice and the Native American Community Academy integrating Native culture throughout the school

article_title: Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development
citation: Rohit Mehra, Samdyuti Suri, Prithviraj K Tagadinamani, Kapil Singi, Vikrant Kaulgud, Adam P. Burden. (2026). Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06101
title: SHIELD: a multi-agent system for embedding incidental learning in developer-agent interactions
description: SHIELD (Safeguarding Human Expertise and Incidental Learning in Software Development) is a multi-agent prototype operating within the developer's IDE alongside their AI coding agent. It instruments the agent to emit telemetry on every code change, then a Telemetry Observer Agent, Learning Orchestrator, Teachability Triage Agent, Probe Generator Agent, Knowledge Assessor Agent, and Microlearning Generator Agent identify genuine knowledge gaps and surface probes and microlearning asynchronously. It is implemented as a VSCode extension using CrewAI, Neo4j for the Concept Map, and GPT-5.1, currently instrumented for Claude Code.
requirements: Requires instrumenting the developer's AI coding agent to emit structured telemetry capturing changes, rationale, alternatives considered, and confidence.
constraints: The current prototype works only with Claude Code as the AI coding agent; no empirical user evaluation has been conducted yet.
target_learners: Professional software developers delegating coding tasks to AI agents
target_learning_goals: Repaying Knowledge Debt by addressing emerging knowledge gaps as they arise without interrupting development flow
examples: A walkthrough shows a developer delegating a webhook retry issue; the agent replaces fixed retry logic with exponential backoff and jitter, and SHIELD surfaces a probe, assesses partial understanding, and delivers microlearning followed by a comprehension check.
key_sources: Rohit Mehra, Samdyuti Suri, Prithviraj K Tagadinamani, Kapil Singi, Vikrant Kaulgud, Adam P. Burden. (2026). Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06101

article_title: Investing in Texas Teacher Preparation: Key Features of Successful Residency Programs
citation: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wei, W. (2024). Investing in Texas teacher preparation: Key features of successful residency programs [Brief]. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/texas-teacher-preparation-brief
title: Structure EPP–district partnerships around shared governance with joint data-informed decision-making
description: Texas interwove responsibility for teacher preparation across educator preparation programs (EPPs) and districts, with grants built on the assumption that the two work in tandem. As the TEA described, "In high-quality teacher residency models, the EPP and [district] have shared ownership over the preparation, support, and success of the teacher resident." Partnership requirements were instantiated through shared governance meetings that specified attendance by both parties, identified topics for collaborative planning, and called for joint data-informed decision-making, creating feedback loops for continuous improvement.
requirements: Shared governance meetings attended by both EPP and district personnel, with joint data-informed decision-making
examples: Shared governance enabled EPPs to iterate on coursework, revisit assignments, and improve alignment to district contexts after practice-based redesigns
key_sources: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wei, W. (2024). Investing in Texas teacher preparation: Key features of successful residency programs [Brief]. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/texas-teacher-preparation-brief

article_title: 'Artificial Intelligence and Communities of Inquiry: Reimagining Educational Experiences'
citation: Stenbom, S., & Garrison, D. R. (2026). Artificial Intelligence and Communities of Inquiry: Reimagining Educational Experiences. The International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning, 27(2), 114–131. https://doi.org/10.19173/irrodl.v27i2.9314
title: Shared metacognition—collective monitoring and management of thinking—as a responsible pathway for engaging critically with AI outputs
description: Shared metacognition is the CoI construct of "collective monitoring and management of thinking." The article argues it "offers a responsible pathway for educators and learners to engage critically with AI-generated outputs, ensuring that technology strengthens rather than supplants collaborative inquiry." It functions as the mechanism by which learning communities keep AI use subordinate to reflective, collaborative inquiry rather than replacing it.
requirements: Educators and learners must collectively monitor and manage their thinking when working with AI-generated outputs
constraints: The pathway is argued theoretically; the article reports no empirical test of it
examples: The article applies shared metacognition to the scenario of learners evaluating AI-generated outputs within a community of inquiry

article_title: Security Education in Higher Education through AI-Powered Gamification
citation: Bingjun Li, Christopher Buzaid, Weihao Qu. (2025). Security Education in Higher Education through AI-Powered Gamification. Journal of Cybersecurity, Digital Forensics and Jurisprudence. https://doi.org/10.65879/3070-5789.2025.01.07
title: Short-video-style micro-learning format delivering security concepts in under 30 seconds
description: This pattern embeds cybersecurity content in fast-paced, TikTok-style filter mini-games suited to mobile devices and students' daily routines. In the Password Thinker game, users choose the stronger of two passwords and must complete five rounds within a total of 20 seconds. The authors describe it as "our first attempt to use short-video filter formats to increase user engagement and deliver essential cybersecurity concepts in under 30 seconds," aligning delivery with fast-paced decision habits.
requirements: Mobile-friendly delivery that fits into students' daily routines
Time constraints that create urgency and mimic real-world mobile usage cognitive load
constraints: The article presents this as a first exploratory attempt; engagement evidence comes from expert votes and self-report rather than measured learning gains
target_learners: digital natives accustomed to short-video platforms
examples: The TikTok Filter Game Password Thinker asks users to pick the stronger password between two options across five rounds in 20 seconds

article_title: It's Not the Tool, It's the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction
citation: Jochen Kuhn, Stefan Küchemann, David J. Rakestraw, & Patrik Vogt. (2026). It's Not the Tool, It's the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction.
title: Shard elevator ride smartphone acceleration dataset with AIRIS-structured student guide
description: A concrete classroom task in which a smartphone recorded vertical acceleration during a downward elevator ride in the Shard (London) from floor 34 to the ground floor, held vertically against the elevator wall so only the y-component is meaningful. The dataset is released with the paper: "the dataset is provided with this paper, and the same AIRIS structure applies to any phenomenon that can be measured, modelled, and interpreted". Students predict, delegate visualization and integration to AI, then interpret and reflect.
requirements: No access to the Shard or any moving vehicle is required because the dataset is supplied
Conceptual knowledge of acceleration, numerical integration, and kinematic relations must be established through prior instruction
constraints: The sensor data required correction for a systematic offset, determined as the mean acceleration during the constant-velocity interval from 15 s to 20 s (a_offset = 0.042 m/s2)
target_learning_goals: characterizing motion from real acceleration data
relating a-t, v-t, and s-t representations
examples: The task guide asks students to estimate maximum speed without AI, then check whether the AI-derived maximum speed matches that estimate
key_sources: Jochen Kuhn, Stefan Küchemann, David J. Rakestraw, & Patrik Vogt. (2026). It's Not the Tool, It's the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13812

article_title: Bayesian cognitive diagnosis optimizes personalized learning paths via mediation of cognitive load and Hidden Markov Model state transitions
citation: Feng Z and Huang K (2026) Bayesian cognitive diagnosis optimizes personalized learning paths via mediation of cognitive load and Hidden Markov Model state transitions. Front. Psychol. 17:1879982. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1879982
title: Shortest remediation path algorithm converting diagnosed knowledge states into prerequisite-respecting learning sequences
description: The shortest remediation path algorithm is "the core technical component of this study for transforming cognitive diagnostic results into personalized learning sequences." It takes a student's current knowledge state vector, a prerequisite graph, and a target state; computes each missing attribute's dependency depth; sorts missing attributes by ascending depth; inserts any missing prerequisites before their dependents; and recommends three unanswered questions per attribute sorted by ascending difficulty. Its design goal is minimum path cost while respecting prerequisite relationships.
requirements: A diagnosed binary knowledge state vector and a directed acyclic prerequisite graph over attributes
A Q-matrix for selecting unanswered practice questions per attribute
constraints: Path cost counts each missing attribute and each inserted prerequisite as one step; efficiency is measured as path length, not learning outcomes
target_learners: online learners with partial attribute mastery diagnosed from response data
undergraduate students in the validation experiment
target_learning_goals: remediating missing cognitive attributes in prerequisite-consistent order toward full mastery
examples: For a student who mastered only A1, the algorithm produced the sequence (A2, A3, A4, A5); for a student who mastered A1 and A2, it moved A4 before A5 to yield [A3, A4, A5].
key_sources: Feng Z and Huang K (2026) Bayesian cognitive diagnosis optimizes personalized learning paths via mediation of cognitive load and Hidden Markov Model state transitions. Front. Psychol. 17:1879982. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1879982

article_title: CLARA: An AI-Augmented Analytics Dashboard for Collaboration Literacy
citation: Dawei Xie, Khalil Anderson, Tochukwu Eze, Chenghong Lin, Bookyung Shin, and Marcelo Worsley. (2026). CLARA: An AI-Augmented Analytics Dashboard for Collaboration Literacy. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17259
title: Human-AI common ground through shared analytics artifacts
description: CLARA is designed around the idea that learners, educators, and AI should reason over the same representations rather than following a generate-and-consume pattern. The article states that "the artifacts sit between the user and the AI, which are visible to both, queryable by both, and interpretable by both", so an educator can point to a concept-map node and the agent can cite a relationship from the same map. This is common ground in a practical sense of shared analytical objects, not full mutual knowledge verified through grounding acts. The framework suggests AI systems should generate representations that become shared working material supporting ongoing inquiry from both sides.
requirements: Artifacts must be visible to, queryable by, and interpretable by both the user and the AI agent
constraints: The article distinguishes this from common ground in the full sense of mutual knowledge verified through grounding acts
target_learners: Learners and educators engaging in collaborative group work
target_learning_goals: Collaboration literacy: interpreting and reflecting on how a group collaborates
examples: In CLARA, a learner or educator viewing a concept map and asking the agent a question works from the same shared reference as the agent, which cites relationships from the same map in its responses

article_title: Testing Our Foundations: Citation Trends, Errors, and Emerging Hallucinations in the Computing Education Literature
citation: Paul Denny, Gweneth Barbre, Musa Blake, Yan Cathy Hua, Juho Leinonen, Andrew Luxton-Reilly, James Prather, and Brent N. Reeves. (2027). Testing Our Foundations: Citation Trends, Errors, and Emerging Hallucinations in the Computing Education Literature. SIGCSE-TS 2027. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16574
title: Shared responsibility model: authors verify every cited work, venues adopt targeted checks and explicit policies, and publishers improve metadata quality
description: The article proposes a shared responsibility model as the way forward against hallucinated references. Authors should verify every cited work, especially when generative AI was used in writing, and should not cite sources they have not personally checked. Reviewers and program committees should not be expected to manually audit every reference; venues can adopt targeted checks for high-risk cases and make policies explicit at submission. Publishers should improve metadata quality and support post-publication correction and reference-validation tools.
requirements: Authors personally verify every cited work before citing it
Automated tools should be human-in-the-loop systems that highlight suspicious references, explain why a reference was flagged, and return feedback to authors before review
constraints: Many suspicious references turn out to be metadata mismatches, valid variants, or human errors rather than hallucinations, so automated checking is not straightforward
Manual checking of references goes beyond what can be expected from reviewers
target_learning_goals: maintaining citation accuracy and research integrity when using generative AI writing tools
examples: The article reports that ACM policy allows retraction for AI-related content-integrity issues, arXiv has proposed bans for fabricated references, and some computing education venues list fabricated references among grounds for desk rejection
key_sources: Paul Denny, Gweneth Barbre, Musa Blake, Yan Cathy Hua, Juho Leinonen, Andrew Luxton-Reilly, James Prather, and Brent N. Reeves. (2027). Testing Our Foundations: Citation Trends, Errors, and Emerging Hallucinations in the Computing Education Literature. SIGCSE-TS 2027. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16574

article_title: EduBehaviors: Assertion-based Schemas for Auditable Coding of Educational Dialogues
citation: Julian Bernado, Ana Trindade Ribeiro, Xander Beberman, and Susanna Loeb. (2026). EduBehaviors: Assertion-Based Schemas for Auditable Coding of Educational Dialogues. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27043
title: Share assertion definitions, annotated examples, trained classifiers, and combination rules so researchers can build on existing annotation work
description: The article recommends making behavioral annotation components reusable and inspectable: an assertion annotated once in a corpus can inform multiple construct labels, and assertion annotations can train smaller classifiers for later annotation. Sharing "assertion definitions, annotated examples, trained classifiers, and combination rules" reduces the need to develop every measure from the beginning, while each reused measure still requires validation for its intended use.
requirements: Assertion annotations must remain inspectable so researchers can assess how assertions contribute to each construct label
constraints: Applying trained classifiers to another corpus requires checking that they identify the intended behaviors in the new setting
target_learners: education researchers measuring teaching practices and student thinking in conversational data
target_learning_goals: reducing repeated development and annotation work across educational construct measures
examples: Identifying whether an educator asks a question can contribute to measures of focusing questions, funneling questions, responses to student mistakes, or relationship building, with other evidence distinguishing these uses
key_sources: Julian Bernado, Ana Trindade Ribeiro, Xander Beberman, and Susanna Loeb. (2026). EduBehaviors: Assertion-Based Schemas for Auditable Coding of Educational Dialogues. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27043

article_title: GenAI assessment and language equity: Drawing the line between support and substitution
citation: Grace Li. (2026). GenAI Assessment and Language Equity: Drawing the Line between Support and Substitution. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09760-1
title: Shift integrity governance from detection to assessment design
description: The article recommends a design-first approach that creates observable learning traces, clarifies what is being assessed, and makes the integrity boundary operational before submission. It argues this 'moves integrity governance away from suspicion and surveillance and toward transparent design and accountable decision-making', creating safe harbours for legitimate language assistance while preserving prohibitions on substitution. Detection-led responses are limited and risk cohort-skewed injustice.
requirements: Assessment designs that make reasoning visible and clarify the construct
Institutional commitment to redesigning assessment rather than relying on tool bans or blanket disclosure
constraints: Detector outputs may have a triage role but rarely constitute proof; over-reliance increases the risk of false positives and cohort-skewed error
target_learners: EAL and multilingual students in higher education
target_learning_goals: Protecting assessment validity and fairness while permitting legitimate language support
examples: Regulators and quality agencies such as TEQSA emphasise that detection-led responses are limited and assessment design must play a central role in learning assurance
key_sources: Grace Li. (2026). GenAI Assessment and Language Equity: Drawing the Line between Support and Substitution. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09760-1

article_title: AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance
citation: Grace Liu, Brian Christian, Tsvetomira Dumbalska, Michiel A. Bakker, Rachit Dubey. (2026). AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance. Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04721
title: Short-sighted AI collaboration: instant-answer assistance erodes persistence via shifted effort reference points and lost metacognitive calibration
description: The article frames current AI systems as "fundamentallyshort-termcollaborators" that provide instant, complete answers and rarely refuse, in contrast to good human collaborators who balance helping with fostering autonomy. It proposes two mechanisms for the observed persistence decline: hedonic-adaptation-like shifting of the reference point for how long a task should take, making unaided work feel counterfactually more effortful and self-reinforcing further offloading; and removal of the productive struggle through which people develop accurate self-knowledge, undermining the metacognitive calibration that sustains persistence. The theory situates the findings within the cognitive offloading and AI-induced deskilling literature.
requirements: AI systems currently optimized for short-term helpfulness and instant answers; the theory explains effects observed after brief (∼10 minute) AI-assisted problem-solving sessions.
constraints: The mechanisms are the authors' interpretation, not directly tested; experiments captured only brief AI exposure, and whether effects accumulate or attenuate with prolonged use remains an open question.
target_learners: Adult online research participants solving fraction and reading-comprehension tasks
Learners using AI assistants for reasoning-intensive tasks
examples: In the experiments, participants given a GPT-5 sidebar assistant for learning problems were then tested without it and showed lower solve rates and higher skip rates than never-assisted controls.

article_title: Governing generative AI in higher education: Emerging policy approaches and support ecosystems at innovative U.S. universities
citation: Qian, Y. (2026). Governing generative AI in higher education: emerging policy approaches and support ecosystems at innovative U.S. Universities. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00233-x
title: Shift academic integrity effort from policing to design by pairing integrity policies with assessment innovation and AI literacy
description: The article recommends that institutions move away from detector-based enforcement toward a pedagogy-first integrity model. It advises investing in "process-rich assignments that include drafts, prompt logs, reflections, oral explanations, and revision histories" and mainstreaming AI literacy as a core academic capability rather than a remediation activity. This principle follows from the study's findings that institutions converge on detector skepticism and AI-literacy support while assignment-redesign resources remain scarce, indicating a gap between guidance and implementation supports.
requirements: Teaching centers and libraries provide templates and workshops that can be scaled into discipline-specific exemplars
Every syllabus carries a clear AI policy with standardized options
constraints: Assessment-redesign strategies increase instructional workload and do not eliminate ambiguity
target_learning_goals: AI literacy as a core academic capability
examples: The article's Table 1 recommends process-rich assignments and notes assignment-redesign resources appeared in only 9 of 50 institutions while pedagogy/assessment design guidance appeared in 44 of 50

citation: Rienties, Bart; Coughlan, Tim; Domingue, John and Herodotou, Christothea (2026). New systems of learning for distance learning institutions? A six-study review of implementing AIDA. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100607
title: Sharples' embedded system approach for GenAI in distance learning organisations
description: An ecological, systems-level framework, built on Bronfenbrenner's Ecological Systems Theory, for how distance learning organisations should approach GenAI. It treats learners' engagement with AI as influenced by layers of interactions with peers, family, learning materials, tutors, student services, IT support, quality assurance, government regulators and tech companies. The article applies it to organise the six AIDA studies, mapping stakeholders and institutional layers, and lists its elements: "build awareness and leadership support, fostering collaborative cultures, using data for decision-making, and a commitment to continuous learning."
requirements: Commitment from both senior management and the work floor
Longitudinal attention to how an innovation embeds over time within the organisation

target_learning_goals: responsible institutional design, deployment and evaluation of GenAI learning support

citation: Melissa E. Hudson and David W. Test. (2011). Evaluating the Evidence Base of Shared Story Reading to Promote Literacy for Students With Extensive Support Needs. Research & Practice for Persons with Severe Disabilities, 36(1-2), 34-45. http://www.education.uncc.edu/access/

Common features include repeated story lines, attention getters, picture symbols paired with words, summarized text with controlled vocabulary, and repeated readings. With older children, lesson content and style reflect age-appropriate literature such as chapters.

citation: Chevalier N., Sheffield T. D., Nelson J. M., Clark C. A. C., Wiebe S. A., Espy K. A. (2012). Underpinnings of the Costs of Flexibility in Preschool Children: The Roles of Inhibition and Working Memory. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3308575/
title: Shape School task with baseline and switch conditions for measuring flexibility components in preschoolers
description: The Shape School is a computerized task in which children name cartoon stimuli by color or shape, conveyed through a story about school activities. It includes a color baseline block (12 test trials), a shape baseline block (6 practice and 12 test trials), and a switch condition (6 practice and 15 test trials) where hatted stimuli cue shape naming and hatless stimuli cue color naming, yielding 10 shift and 4 no-shift trials. The article selected it because it "contains both baseline and mixed-task blocks, and has demonstrated psychometric reliability and validity." Accuracy was coded from videorecorded sessions with 93.83% inter-rater agreement.
requirements: Stimuli must dissociate color and shape dimensions to reduce perseveration in 3-year-olds
Examiner-paced trial progression to accommodate young children's response speeds
constraints: The fixed condition order and limited trial count prevented modeling dimension (color vs. shape) effects on switch costs
target_learning_goals: assessing cognitive flexibility, including goal representation and switch implementation components
examples: Children completed the color baseline, shape baseline, and switch conditions in a single videorecorded laboratory session

article_title: Navigating Windows Into Past Human Minds: A Framework of Shifting Selves in Historical Perspective Taking
citation: Nilsen, A. P. (2016). Navigating windows into past human minds: A framework of shifting selves in historical perspective taking. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 25, 372-410. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2016.1160830
title: Framework of four shifting self perspectives in historical perspective taking
description: The article proposes that historical perspective taking involves four self perspectives, each with distinct grammatical features: the now-self (present-day first-person statements), the hypothetical past self (first-person conditionals), the imagined past self (first-person present indicative not referring to the present-day self), and the timeless generalized other (generic you, we, people). The framework links HPT to social science research on perspective taking and the self, and is used to analyze how learners process historical material. As the abstract states, "Four shifting “self perspectives” were identified, whereby participants thought as their present-day selves, constructed hypothetical and imagined past selves, and made timeless generalizations about humans."
requirements: Think-aloud or other discourse data in which grammatical forms (pronouns, verb mood, tense) can be analyzed to identify which self perspective is active
constraints: Developed from a small qualitative study of four Stanford undergraduates or recent graduates; the article frames it as an exploratory study that generalizes to theory rather than to populations
examples: Coding every transcript segment against Table 2 criteria, e.g. Callie's conditional "I would probably just feel really betrayed" coded as hypothetical past self

citation: Damşa, C. I. (2014). The multi-layered nature of small-group learning: Productive interactions in object-oriented collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. (2014) 9:247–281. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9193-8
title: Shared epistemic agency as an emerging, group-level capacity for deliberate joint object-oriented interaction
description: The article defines shared epistemic agency as "the capacity to enable a deliberate, joint, object-oriented interaction." The epistemic aspect refers to the group's active involvement with knowledge and its materialization into knowledge objects; sharedness means agency is expressed in joint efforts at the group level, not in each individual member's pursuits. Agency is treated as an emerging, recursive capacity that manifests and unfolds during interaction, drawing on the view that epistemic agency emerges through participation in collective activities rather than residing in the individual mind.
requirements: Intersubjectivity and interaction between participants
Sustained active participation in collective knowledge work
constraints: The construct was analyzed by qualifying sequences of actions showing deliberate, strategic, and reflective conduct within the studied project setting
target_learning_goals: taking initiative in inquiry and knowledge construction
joint management of collaborative research processes
examples: Groups manifesting shared epistemic agency produced knowledge objects that were more complex and suitable to the problems addressed

article_title: Beyond folk theories of CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). Beyond folk theories of CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9098-0
title: Shared dynamic dialogic space as focal point of children's collective reasoning around interactive whiteboards
description: Drawing on the Kershner, Mercer, Warwick and Kleine Staarman study of elementary students using interactive whiteboards during small-group collaborative discussions, the editorial describes an extension of distributed cognition with "the metaphor of a shared dynamic dialogic space as the focal point of the children's collective reasoning and co-construction of knowledge". The whiteboard functions as a location for focusing shared attention, a referential center for exploratory talk, an external memory, common ground, indexical source for group cognition, and visual foundation for group identity; teacher-instilled 'talk rules' help structure this space.

target_learners: Elementary students working in small groups
target_learning_goals: Collaborative reasoning and co-construction of shared knowledge
examples: The editorial also calls the construct the 'joint problem space', a way of thinking about how critical dimensions of CSCL interactions come together.

article_title: CSCL artifacts
citation: G. Stahl & S. Ludvigsen & N. Law & U. Cress. (2014). CSCL artifacts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 9, 237–245. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9200-0
title: Shared epistemic agency observable in interaction, including referred agency embedded in designed artifacts
description: Building on Emirbayer and Mische, the editorial treats agency as observable in interaction rather than a hypothetical psychological state, and extends it to groups and artifacts: 'Designed artifacts exercise a referred agency, designed into the form of the artifact by the intentions of the designer — and visible in that form.' Interaction can then be viewed as an inter-action among many sources of agency converging in a concrete situation. Group members orient the group subtly toward projected joint goals.
requirements: Agency must be analyzed in excerpts of productive interaction, not inferred as an internal state
constraints: The article notes this does not necessarily involve a rationalist sub-goal hierarchy

target_learning_goals: negotiating, reflecting on and carrying out joint action objectives
examples: A software developer embeds goals in software that determine to some extent how it can and cannot be used

article_title: Could probability be out of proportion? Self-explanation and example-based practice help students with lower proportional reasoning skills learn probability
citation: Begolli, K. N., Dai, T., McGinn, K. M., & Booth, J. L. (2021). Could probability be out of proportion? Self-explanation and example-based practice help students with lower proportional reasoning skills learn probability. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09550-9
title: Shared-root account of proportional and probabilistic reasoning schemata
description: The article frames two competing accounts of the proportion–probability connection: one in which "the conceptual schema of probabilities is separate from that of proportions" and another "where both schemata (probabilities and proportions) stem from the same root" (Fischbein & Gazit, 1984; Piaget & Inhelder, 1975). The study's findings—prior proportional reasoning predicting probabilistic learning and lower-proportion students benefiting most from example-based practice—are presented as supporting the shared-root account. Proportional reasoning is treated as integral to analyzing sample spaces, quantifying probabilities proportionally, and using correlations.
requirements: Learners must encounter probability problems whose solution requires proportional comparison and quantification for the shared schema to be exercised
constraints: The authors note the theoretical accounts on conceptual representations remain unsettled; the evidence is correlational plus one intervention
examples: The study tested the account in regular seventh-grade classrooms using the Connected Mathematics Project What Do You Expect? probability unit

article_title: Do New Forms of Reading Pay Off? A Meta-Analysis on the Relationship Between Leisure Digital Reading Habits and Text Comprehension
citation: Altamura, L., Vargas, C., & Salmerón, L. (2023). Do New Forms of Reading Pay Off? A Meta-Analysis on the Relationship Between Leisure Digital Reading Habits and Text Comprehension. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543231216463
title: Shallowing versus displacement hypotheses as competing accounts of digital reading habits' comprehension payoff
description: The article frames two competing explanatory accounts for how leisure digital reading habits relate to comprehension. The displacement hypothesis holds that "time previously devoted to print reading may just be replaced by time devoted to digital reading", predicting a positive association comparable to print. The shallowing hypothesis holds that frequent use of ultra-brief social media promotes rapid, relatively shallow thought, so short-length, fast-paced, low linguistic-quality digital texts foster scanning and skimming rather than deep processing. The authors state their results do not support displacement and tentatively favor shallowing as an explanation for the small pooled effect.
requirements: The account applies to leisure (not academic or work-related) digital reading habits measured via self-report frequency questionnaires in correlational studies.
constraints: The authors state they can only speculate about the divergent patterns, since the primary studies are correlational and cannot establish causal mechanisms.
target_learners: readers across the lifespan, from primary school students to university students and adults
examples: The meta-analysis tested the displacement prediction of a positive association and the shallowing prediction of negative-to-null effect sizes against the pooled r = .055 and the stage moderation pattern.

title: Shiny App for finding optimal designs in classroom climate studies
description: An interactive web application the authors created "to help researchers plan classroom climate studies and learn about optimal designs and the impact of the quantities that need to be considered when planning such studies." It has two tabs corresponding to the two scenarios: maximizing power under a fixed budget and minimizing the budget for a given power level. With default values (budget 20,000€, costs 68.20€ and 7.05€, ICC(1)s and slopes .2), it returns 130 classes, 12 students per class, and 98% power in Scenario 1, and 61 classes, 12 students, and a budget of 9,311€ in Scenario 2.

target_learning_goals: Study planning and power analysis for multilevel latent variable classroom climate studies

article_title: Observational, student, and teacher perspectives on interpersonal teacher behavior: Shared and unique associations with teacher and student emotions
citation: Donker, M. H., van Vemde, L., Hessen, D. J., van Gog, T., & Mainhard, T. (2021). Observational, student, and teacher perspectives on interpersonal teacher behavior: Shared and unique associations with teacher and student emotions. Learning and Instruction, vol. 73, 101414. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2020.101414
title: Novel regression-based correction method for splitting shared and unique explained variance of multiple predictors
description: The article introduces a novel statistical approach based on multiple regression that "allows to calculate the explained variance of different combinations of predictors, and the shared and unique variance of each (set of) predictors", even in the case of suppressor effects or large overlap between variables. It works by correcting the explained variance in several steps, combining information from various multiple regression analyses with one, two, or three predictors; an explanation and the R code are provided in Appendix B. The empirical part of the paper serves as an illustration of the method with data on teacher interpersonal behavior and emotions.

constraints: Simple addition and subtraction of effects only leads to correct calculation of shared and unique parts when there are no suppressor effects
target_learning_goals: separating shared and unique variance of raters or perspectives predicting outcomes
examples: Applied to 76 teachers' data to split variance of observer, student, and teacher perspectives predicting teacher and student positive and negative emotions

article_title: Reading comprehension on handheld devices versus on paper: A narrative review and meta-analysis of the medium effect and its moderators.
citation: Salmerón, L., Altamura, L., Delgado, P., Karagiorgi, A., & Vargas, C. (2023). Reading comprehension on handheld devices vs. on paper: A narrative review and meta-analysis of the medium effect and its moderators. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/edu0000830
title: Shallowing hypothesis as an explanatory account of the screen inferiority effect
description: The review presents the shallowing hypothesis (Annisette & Lafreniere, 2017) as one of the most influential theoretical accounts of the screen inferiority effect. It "assumes that typical interactions with digital devices involve quick episodes with short pieces of texts, which favors a mindset aiming to browse as much information as possible, without in-depth elaboration." When reading on a digital device, readers may activate this shallow mindset and allocate cognitive resources less efficiently, which should be most visible in challenging contexts demanding self-regulation. The review uses it to generate moderator predictions, several of which existing evidence does not support.
requirements: As an account, it presupposes that digital reading habits transfer a browsing-oriented mindset to comprehension tasks
constraints: The review notes existing evidence does not support the prediction of higher screen inferiority for older students, and similar comprehension on tablets versus e-readers does not support it for handheld devices
target_learners: readers across ages who use digital devices, from primary students to undergraduates
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of print and digital texts
examples: The review derived moderator predictions from the hypothesis, including larger effects for expository texts, longer texts, scrolling, tablets, time limits, and group settings.

article_title: Students’ motivational trajectories and academic success in math-intensive study programs: Why short-term motivational assessments matter.
citation: Daria Katharina Benden and Fani Lauermann. (2021). Students' Motivational Trajectories and Academic Success in Math-Intensive Study Programs: Why Short-Term Motivational Assessments Matter. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000708
title: Use short-term motivational assessments as early warning signs of academic struggles and course dropout in math-intensive fields
description: The article recommends that educators and researchers consider short-term motivational changes as early indicators of later academic difficulties. The authors state that "short-term declines in students' expectancy and value beliefs—especially at the beginning of college—are a precursor to later declines in academic performance, and can thus function as early warning signs of academic struggles and intentions to leave college." Their own data support this: motivational changes in the first weeks predicted end-of-term satisfaction, exam performance, and dropout.

constraints: Most existing research has used only two or three measurement points, limiting understanding of trajectory shape and sensitive time points

target_learning_goals: Early identification of students at risk of academic struggle and course dropout
examples: Study 1b assessed students weekly in the first four weeks of the semester and found the motivational shock between Weeks 2 and 3 predicted end-of-term outcomes.

Time limits short enough that even the brightest pupils cannot complete everything

article_title: How the predictors of math achievement change over time: A longitudinal machine learning approach.
citation: Lavelle-Hill, R., Frenzel, A. C., Goetz, T., Lichtenfeld, S., Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Sakaki, M., Smith, G., & Murayama, K. (2024). How the Predictors of Math Achievement Change Over Time: A Longitudinal Machine Learning Approach. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(8), 1383–1403. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000863
title: SHAP-based variable importance for interpreting achievement prediction models
description: Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) values are a post hoc, model-agnostic interpretation method used in this article to quantify which variables and variable groups predict math achievement and how their importance changes over time. The authors argue SHAP has three key benefits: it indicates each predictor's direction of contribution, it is computed per individual student enabling heterogeneity analysis, and it is additive so it aggregates to sample-level importance. Group importance was computed by summing absolute SHAP values across variables within theoretically defined predictor groups.

Grouping of predictors into conceptually similar sets to yield stable, interpretable group importance scores
constraints: Variable importance depends on the model and calculation method and should be interpreted with caution
Importance values are unlikely to reflect only causal effects given reciprocal influences among predictors
target_learning_goals: identifying which predictors contribute to math achievement predictions
examples: The article states: "we argue that SHAP values have three key benefits: (a) They indicate the direction in which each predictor contributes to the prediction (i.e., whether there is a positive or negative predictive relationship)"

article_title: Reading comprehension in L1 and L2 readers: neurocomputational mechanisms revealed through large language models
citation: Gu, C., Nastase, S. A., Zada, Z., & Li, P. (2025). Reading comprehension in L1 and L2 readers: neurocomputational mechanisms revealed through large language models. npj Science of Learning, 10:46. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00337-y
title: Shared computational principles between LLMs and human language processing, refined by individual differences
description: The article works within the framework that LLMs and human brains share computational principles for language processing, centered on the "principle of context-speciﬁc embedding", which "posits that preceding context is actively engaged in word comprehension during language processes". GPT-2 contextual embeddings serve as explicit linguistic features in encoding models whose alignment with brain responses indexes this shared processing. The study refines the framework by showing alignment depends on readers' linguistic, attentional, and language-experience characteristics.
requirements: LLM-based encoding models with contextual embeddings and naturalistic reading data with explicit comprehension measures
constraints: The study used only GPT-2; the authors note variations in model architecture may lead to distinct patterns of model-brain associations
examples: Encoding models built from the eighth layer of GPT-2 predicted brain responses recorded during self-paced reading of five expository texts with simultaneous fMRI and eye-tracking

article_title: Electrocortical correlates of attention differentiate individual capacity in associative learning
citation: Raynal, E., Schipper, K., Brandner, C., Ruggeri, P. & Barral, J. (2024). Electrocortical correlates of attention differentiate individual capacity in associative learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00236-8
title: Trial-and-error shape–color associative learning task scored with Signal Detection Theory d'
description: A computerized associative learning task in which 12 abstract two-dimensional shapes had to be associated with one of four colors through trial-and-error feedback, with yes/no responses to target or lure color-shape pairings. Performance is scored with the Signal Detection Theory index d', which the authors chose because it "allows us to assess the impact of attentional processes on perceptual sensitivity" while minimizing response bias. The task was designed to avoid ceiling effects in non-clinical populations and permits SDT indices over classical behavioral measures.
requirements: Difficulty must be calibrated to the sample population; associations count as learned once responses within the last 48 trials exceed 95% correct
constraints: The task was demanding: 19 participants failed to reach the criterion within the 504-trial maximum
The task may exhibit a directional response bias; the authors suggest a counterbalanced response-button design could mitigate this
examples: Participants completed a minimum of 360 trials with 1000 ms visual feedback (Correct, False, or Too slow) after each response

article_title: Prevalence of undiagnosed dyslexia in African-American primary school children
citation: Laura Cassidy, Kayla Reggio, Bennett A. Shaywitz and Sally E. Shaywitz. (2023). Prevalence of undiagnosed dyslexia in African-American primary school children. npj Science of Learning 8:52. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00204-8
title: Shaywitz DyslexiaScreen: a brief teacher-completed dyslexia screener with high ROC AUC for grades K-2
description: The Shaywitz DyslexiaScreen is "a series of questions posed to the teachers based on age appropriate skills dealing with the interface of oral and written language (phonological processing)" and "is not a test or assessment tool requiring a response by the student." It is brief, completed independently by the teacher on a tablet, based on the teacher's observations after months with the child, and was used in this study for universal screening in two New Orleans charter schools.
requirements: Completed by the child's teacher who ideally has spent months with each child in the classroom; teachers received an intensive training session on dyslexia by a Certified Academic Language Therapist
target_learners: Children in kindergarten through second grade
target_learning_goals: Early identification of children at risk for dyslexia
examples: Used in early spring 2018 to screen 246 K-2 children in two New Orleans charter schools; 121 (49.2%) screened at risk.
key_sources: Laura Cassidy, Kayla Reggio, Bennett A. Shaywitz and Sally E. Shaywitz. (2023). Prevalence of undiagnosed dyslexia in African-American primary school children. npj Science of Learning 8:52. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00204-8

article_title: Shared effects of one’s own and others’ experiences during reinforcement learning on episodic memory
citation: Maria A. Woitow, Anthony I. Jang, Ben Eppinger, Matthew R. Nassar, Marcel Brass & Julia M. Rodriguez Buritica. (2026). Shared effects of one's own and others' experiences during reinforcement learning on episodic memory. npj Science of Learning 11:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00409-7
title: Shared encoding mechanisms: experienced and vicarious RPE signaling influence episodic memory in comparable ways
description: The article proposes that reward prediction errors generated during one's own choices and during observation of another player's choices feed into episodic memory encoding through shared mechanisms. It reports that "positive image RPEs were associated with enhanced memory" in both learning conditions, and that gambling positively modulated the RPE-memory relationship independent of condition. The account aligns with prior work pointing to similarities in RPE signaling during learning from one's own and others' choices and feedback, while allowing that subjective memory strength still favors experiential learning.
requirements: A task in which memory items are presented at the reward-predictive stage so that image RPEs are temporally coupled with the item to be encoded
constraints: The article found no direct effect of signed image RPEs on memory; the enhancing effect emerged only for positive RPEs in gambling or observed-gambling trials
Feedback-stage RPEs showed no memory effect, attributed to the timing of memory item presentation
target_learners: young adults in laboratory decision-making tasks
target_learning_goals: episodic memory for stimuli encountered during reinforcement learning from own and others' experiences
examples: Participants learned reward probabilities through their own play-or-pass choices and through observing a simulated other player's choices, then completed a surprise recognition memory test
key_sources: Maria A. Woitow, Anthony I. Jang, Ben Eppinger, Matthew R. Nassar, Marcel Brass & Julia M. Rodriguez Buritica. (2026). Shared effects of one's own and others' experiences during reinforcement learning on episodic memory. npj Science of Learning 11:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00409-7

article_title: Behavioral and eye-tracking investigation of event segmentation following short video watching
citation: Li, H., Li, J., Hao, X., & Liu, W. (2025). Behavioral and eye-tracking investigation of event segmentation following short video watching. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00378-3
title: Habitual exposure to short-form media may hinder students' ability to build structured mental representations from extended learning materials
description: The article draws an educational implication from its event-segmentation findings: effective learning from extended materials such as a lecture or textbook relies on segmenting continuous information into a coherent structure, and the segmentation impairment observed after short-video exposure suggests that habitual exposure to short-form media may interfere with building these structured mental representations, potentially affecting comprehension and long-term retention. The authors state this as a caution for educational contexts rather than a tested instructional manipulation.
requirements: Learning tasks that require segmenting a continuous flow of information (e.g., lectures, textbooks)
constraints: The study tested university students immediately after acute exposure; persistence of the effect and generalization to classroom learning remain untested
target_learning_goals: Comprehension and long-term retention of extended, continuous learning materials
examples: The authors propose future research use more emotionally neutral and educationally relevant video clips, such as recordings from real-life educational lectures, as memory encoding material
key_sources: Li, H., Li, J., Hao, X., & Liu, W. (2025). Behavioral and eye-tracking investigation of event segmentation following short video watching. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00378-3

article_title: Regular rhythmic primes improve sentence repetition in children with developmental language disorder
citation: Fiveash, A., Ladányi, E., Camici, J., Chidiac, K., Bush, C. T., Canette, L.-H., Bedoin, N., Gordon, R. L. & Tillmann, B. (2023). Regular rhythmic primes improve sentence repetition in children with developmental language disorder. npj Science of Learning 8:23. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00170-1
title: Shared rhythm–grammar processing mechanisms account for rhythmic priming effects
description: The article frames rhythmic priming within the hypothesis that "engaging the beat-based rhythm processing system impacts subsequent language processing via shared underlying mechanisms". It draws on dynamic attending theory — endogenous neural oscillations synchronize with a regular beat and persist after the rhythm stops — and on the Processing Rhythm in Speech and Music (PRISM) framework, which posits that rhythm and language share facets of neural and cognitive processing. The sentence repetition benefit after regular primes, together with the null on a non-grammatical task, is treated as consistent with this account.
requirements: Priming effects require rhythmic stimulation before a language task with a grammar component
constraints: The exact mechanisms remain open: the authors call for research with other language tasks and neural methods to better understand the mechanisms underlying the priming phenomenon
target_learners: Children aged 5.4–13 years with developmental language disorder
target_learning_goals: Syntactic processing and complex sentence repetition
examples: Regular 32-s musical primes with a 500-ms inter-beat interval in 4/4 meter preceded spoken sentences with subject- and object-relative clauses
key_sources: Fiveash, A., Ladányi, E., Camici, J., Chidiac, K., Bush, C. T., Canette, L.-H., Bedoin, N., Gordon, R. L. & Tillmann, B. (2023). Regular rhythmic primes improve sentence repetition in children with developmental language disorder. npj Science of Learning 8:23. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00170-1

article_title: Keep Me in the Loop: Real-Time Feedback with Multimodal Data
citation: Di Mitri, D., Schneider, J., & Drachsler, H. (2022). KeepMeInTheLoop: Real-Time Feedback with Multimodal Data. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2022) 32:1093–1118. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00281-z
title: SharpFlow: open-source Python tool for offline training and real-time classification of chest compressions
description: SharpFlow is a Python script developed by the authors for data processing in the CPR Tutor, with code available on GitHub. It is "used for offline training and validation of the mistake detection classifiers and the real-time classification of the single CCs", loading MLT-JSON sessions into Pandas data frames, resampling and scaling sensor data, and running a TCP server that feeds data chunks to the stacked LSTM models.
requirements: min-max scaler and LSTM models loaded from memory
TCP connection with the CPR Tutor client
constraints: Classification relies on batch data chunks pushed at the end of each chest compression rather than continuous streaming
target_learning_goals: detecting CPR training mistakes from multimodal sensor data
examples: The authors released SharpFlow on GitHub (https://github.com/dimstudio/SharpFlow) and used it to classify chest compressions in about 70 milliseconds

article_title: Beyond Predictive Learning Analytics Modelling and onto Explainable Artificial Intelligence with Prescriptive Analytics and ChatGPT
citation: Teo Susnjak. (2024). Beyond Predictive Learning Analytics Modelling and onto Explainable Artificial Intelligence with Prescriptive Analytics and ChatGPT. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34:452–482. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00336-3
title: SHAP and Anchors as complementary XAI tools for global interpretability and local-level explainability of at-risk predictions
description: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanation), based on Shapley values from game theory, generates both global interpretability (Step 4) and local explainability (Step 5), addressing the "how" and "why" questions around model behaviour. Anchors complements it at local level: "Anchors reduces a black-box model into a human-readable set of predicates resembling a degenerate decision tree." The article describes SHAP's advantage as detailed quantification of each feature's effect on predictions, while Anchors produces succinct, human-readable rule-based approximations of the underlying complex model's behaviour.
requirements: A trained black-box predictive model whose behaviour the surrogate tools approximate
Both techniques construct surrogate or proxy models simulating the primary model's behaviour
constraints: Both are approximations of the underlying model rather than exact accounts of its mechanics
target_learners: stakeholders including academic advisors, student support teams, and institutions using at-risk predictions
target_learning_goals: validating specific predictions before interventions and explaining to students how and why they were identified as at-risk
examples: Local explainability was demonstrated with two hypothetical students (Student A and Student B) predicted non-completion with probabilities of 97% and 90% respectively, using SHAP force-style plots interpreted as a tug-of-war

article_title: Choice-based Personalization in MOOCs: Impact on Activity and Perceived Value
citation: Ilana Ram, Sara Harris, & Ido Roll. (2024). Choice-based Personalization in MOOCs: Impact on Activity and Perceived Value. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00334-5
title: Shared map of learner-contributed climate issue summaries embedded in MOOC assignments
description: A shared map, implemented with ZeeMaps and embedded in each assignment page, where learners marked a location and pasted their assignment contribution so peers could browse climate issues identified by other learners. There were two maps overall, one per condition. The authors state that "Sharing personal contributions serves two goals: first, it allows the courses to capitalize on the vast knowledge of its learners. Second, it can support learners in identifying peers with similar background." The map service did not capture detailed logfiles, so learner use of the resource was not evaluated.
requirements: Learners submit their contribution to the map with a location mark or place name plus a text box entry
constraints: The tool did not log repeated visits after submission, so the current work did not evaluate how learners used the map
target_learners: MOOC learners across diverse geographic locations
target_learning_goals: Sharing personally relevant knowledge with the course community
examples: Assignment 1 submissions were posted to a shared map of rising-sea-level and local climate impact summaries
