article_title: Towards Automatically Detecting Whether Student Learning is Shallow
citation: Gowda, S. M., Baker, R. S., Corbett, A. T., & Rossi, L. M. (2013). Towards Automatically Detecting Whether Student Learning is Shallow. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0006-4
title: Operational distinction between shallow learning, robust learning, and no learning
description: The article proposes that failure to achieve robust learning takes two distinct forms: no learning at all, or shallow learning—"learning that applies only to the current skill, and does not support transfer or PFL". Shallow learners "may learn the exact skills presented in the tutor, but who do not learn in a robust fashion". The construct is operationalized as the difference between a student's problem-solving post-test score and their transfer or PFL test score, with higher problem-solving performance indicating shallow learning. This distinction matters because the two groups need different interventions: students not yet robust may need more practice, while shallow learners need support building conceptual understanding.
requirements: Tests of both the exact tutor material and of robust learning (transfer or PFL) to compute the score difference used as the ground-truth label
constraints: The operational definition assumes approximately equal average performance across tests so percent-correct scores can be compared directly
target_learners: college students learning genetics problem solving in an intelligent tutoring system
target_learning_goals: distinguishing shallow from robust learning to enable differentiated support
examples: 25 of 71 students were labeled no-transfer-shallow learners, with an average 0.11 point difference between problem-solving and transfer scores
key_sources: Gowda, S. M., Baker, R. S., Corbett, A. T., & Rossi, L. M. (2013). Towards Automatically Detecting Whether Student Learning is Shallow. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0006-4

article_title: Shared Mental Models in Support of Adaptive Instruction for Teams Using the GIFT Tutoring Architecture
citation: J. D. Fletcher & Robert A. Sottilare. (2018). Shared Mental Models in Support of Adaptive Instruction for Teams Using the GIFT Tutoring Architecture. Int J Artif Intell Educ 28:265–285. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0147-y
title: Shared mental models as organized knowledge structures enabling team prediction, explanation, and coordination
description: The article defines shared mental models as the descriptions, explanations, and predictions of team behavior held in common by team members, drawing on Rouse and Morris and Cannon-Bowers et al. It presents them as dynamic cognitive activities rooted in team member interactions rather than static products. The article proposes that ITSs augment individual learner models with these shared models to enable adaptive team instruction, listing seven functions they serve, including "Timing functions that influence how activity is paced" and "Systems-monitoring functions that enable the adjustment of team and member activities in response to errors and omissions".
requirements: Team members must hold models in common; the article states success of interdependent teams "depends on the extent to which this model sharing occurs"
constraints: The article focuses on cognitive factors in small teams and leaves non-cognitive factors and teams of teams for separate consideration
target_learners: interdependent teams such as squads, crews, seminars, and classroom teams
target_learning_goals: shared understanding of roles and responsibilities
examples: The article's Table 1 football example shows a Center's responsibilities, shared knowledge, and assessments structured as hierarchical concepts in GIFT
key_sources: J. D. Fletcher & Robert A. Sottilare. (2018). Shared Mental Models in Support of Adaptive Instruction for Teams Using the GIFT Tutoring Architecture. Int J Artif Intell Educ 28:265–285. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0147-y

article_title: An Intelligent Tutor for Planning in Large Partially Observable Environments
citation: Heindrich, L., Consul, S., & Lieder, F. (2025). An Intelligent Tutor for Planning in Large Partially Observable Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3095–3127. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00493-7
title: Shaping method for teaching cognitive strategies through graduated task complexity
description: A training curriculum inspired by Skinner's method of successive approximations in which "the training starts with a minimal version of the planning task, and as the training progresses, the planning task becomes increasingly more similar to the scenario in which people's planning strategies shall be improved." Complexity increases along two dimensions simultaneously: the number of planning operations the learner chooses between and the size of the environment. This prevents the slow, frustrating learning that occurs when learners face many possible actions in large environments from the start, reducing errors and delay penalties during early learning.
requirements: Smaller versions of the target environment that preserve its structural properties
A mechanism for selecting meaningful choices with different VOC values
constraints: The choice set must always include the optimal planning operation
The number of offered choices is limited (2–4 in the experiment)
examples: Training progressed from an 8-node environment with 2 choices, through 16-node (3 choices) and 30-node (4 choices), to the full 60-node environment over 12 trials
key_sources: Heindrich, L., Consul, S., & Lieder, F. (2025). An Intelligent Tutor for Planning in Large Partially Observable Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3095–3127. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00493-7

article_title: Scientific habits of arguing minds: enhancing online argumentation to foster SHOM
citation: Çakiroğlu, Ü., Güven, O., Yaman, H., & Mazlum Güven, E. (2025). Scientific habits of arguing minds: enhancing online argumentation to foster SHOM. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10474-1
title: Scientific Habits of Mind framework (Çalık & Coll)
description: SHOM characterizes how scientists think through habits including "skepticism, objectivity, rationality, suspension of belief, open-mindedness, mistrust of judgment from authority, and curiosity" (Gauld, 2005), elaborated with key features by Çalık and Coll (2012). The study uses this framework and its 32-item, seven-subscale survey to measure whether online argumentation fosters teacher candidates' SHOM.
requirements: Assessment via the reliable and valid SHOM Survey developed by Çalık and Coll (2012)
examples: Table 1 of the article lists key features of each habit, e.g. suspension of belief as holding in abeyance when evidence is insufficient
key_sources: Çakiroğlu, Ü., Güven, O., Yaman, H., & Mazlum Güven, E. (2025). Scientific habits of arguing minds: enhancing online argumentation to foster SHOM. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10474-1

article_title: Creation in shifting to digital
citation: Patricia A. Young. (2021). Creation in shifting to digital. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09958-7
title: Three emerging themes of shifting to digital: datafication, convergence and personalized learning
description: The editorial organizes one scholarly response to the Jastudy study around three themes of "shifting to digital": datafication, convergence and personalized learning. Fulton, Hoffman and Paek "approach the article from a research perspective and view the CALL system from three emerging themes related to 'shifting to digital': datafication, convergence and personalized learning." This tripartite framework frames how a CALL system can be examined as a digital-creation artifact.
requirements: The framework is used to structure a research-perspective critique of a CALL system study.
constraints: The editorial only announces the themes; it does not elaborate them.
target_learners: Chinese-speaking second language learners of Japanese
target_learning_goals: Japanese functional expression learning supported by CALL systems
examples: The special issue pairs this thematic critique with a separate cultural-perspective response by Shortt.

article_title: Integrating cognition, self-regulation, motivation, and metacognition: a framework of post-pandemic flipped classroom design
citation: Yan Shen, Dan Spencer, Jennifer Tagsold, Hyunsong Kim. (2025). Integrating cognition, self-regulation, motivation, and metacognition: a framework of post-pandemic flipped classroom design. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10485-y
title: Integrated flipped classroom design framework combining FL cycles, SRL cycles, and metacognitive FC orientation
description: The article proposes a conceptual framework of FC design with three main aspects: Flipped Learning (FL) Cycle, Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) Cycle, and Metacognitive FC Orientation. It is founded on interconnected theories — First Principles of Instruction, Self-Regulated Learning, the MUSIC Model of Academic Motivation, and Metacognition — because "a successful flipped classroom requires not only effective and engaging instructions and activities, but also self-regulated and motivated learners with metacognitive awareness." The FL cycle comprises online, in-class, and after-class stages; SRL cycles run in parallel with Proactive Planning, Performance Monitoring, and Learning Reflection stages; and orientation develops students' metacognitive knowledge about FC tasks, strategies, and themselves as learners.
requirements: Requires integration of the three SRL phases with recurring pre-class, in-class, and after-class learning activities to develop students' self-regulation skills required in FC
Requires effective FC design guided by a robust instructional design framework grounded in learning theories
constraints: The authors state there are no existing FC studies that have fully implemented the entire framework; supporting evidence comes from three studies that incorporated one or multiple design aspects
target_learning_goals: active learning and higher-order thinking skills
key_sources: Yan Shen, Dan Spencer, Jennifer Tagsold, Hyunsong Kim. (2025). Integrating cognition, self-regulation, motivation, and metacognition: a framework of post-pandemic flipped classroom design. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10485-y

article_title: Fostering self-regulation in training complex cognitive tasks
citation: Ludo W. van Meeuwen, Saskia Brand-Gruwel, Paul A. Kirschner, Jeano J. P. R. de Bock, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer. (2018). Fostering self-regulation in training complex cognitive tasks. Education Tech Research Dev 66, 53–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9539-9
title: Gradually shift control over task selection from coach to student to foster SRL skills and self-efficacy
description: In a shared control learning environment, the student and the coach share responsibility for future learning, and responsibility gradually shifts from coach to student. The article argues this gives students positive mastery experiences with tasks that fit their learning needs: "Shared control in which the responsibility of the control gradually shift from coach to student will have a positive effect not only on the SRL skills of the students, but will also beneﬁt students' self-efﬁcacy". The study operationalized this through portfolio-based worksheets and coaching meetings.
requirements: Students must be given the opportunity to take initiative in regulating their learning
Learning tasks must be selected that optimally fit individual learning needs
SRL skills must be developed before full control is handed over
constraints: In this study students did not experience freedom in task selection; the authors recommend future research on shared control task-selection designs with feedback
target_learners: Vocational and professional trainees in complex cognitive domains
examples: Worksheets and self-reports prepared students for briefings and progression report meetings so they could contribute from their own point of view and experience control over their learning process

article_title: Shifting to digital: informing the rapid development, deployment, and future of teaching and learning
citation: Lin Lin, Tristan Johnson. (2021). Shifting to digital: informing the rapid development, deployment, and future of teaching and learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09960-z
title: Shifting to Digital special issue (ETR&D)
description: A special issue of ETR&D, the flagship journal of AECT, created during the COVID-19 pandemic to 'provide insights into the applications of relevant research informing the rapid development, deployment and future of teaching and learning'. Guest editors identified 17 papers published at ETR&D in the past five years as anchors, and close to a hundred essays responded to them. The editors state the goal 'was not to select a set of best papers by any means, but to use the papers as anchors for creating dialogue'.
requirements: Guest editors who communicate with potential authors and reviewers and oversee review processes
A call for papers disseminated through newsletter, listserv, websites, and social media
constraints: The 17 anchor papers were selected for relevance to online or digital learning, relevance to rapid deployment, impact factor, scope, and appeal to a wide and diverse population
target_learning_goals: integrating digital technologies into teaching practices during rapid shifts
examples: Guest editors included Drs. Dickson-Deane, Ilgaz, Ioannou, Kimmons, Morel, Natividad, Istenič Starčič, Wijekumar, and Young, with Dr. Istenič Starčič as lead guest editor

article_title: The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic
citation: van Niekerk, J.F. (2015). The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic. Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University.
title: Present learning as short, focused activities within a challenging but non-threatening environment
description: The dissertation reports the primacy-recency effect, whereby material presented first is remembered best and the middle of a lesson least, and recommends "limiting cognitive activities to periods of 5 to 10 minutes each" to minimise low-impact middle-of-lesson learning. It also holds that "Learning is enhanced by challenge and inhibited by threat": perceived threat triggers downshift and a fight-or-flight response that closes connections to the prefrontal cortex and impairs logical thinking.
requirements: Content must be challenging enough to engage curiosity but delivered non-threateningly, with learners feeling secure
constraints: What constitutes a threat differs from person to person; a problem challenging for one learner may threaten another
target_learners: higher education students in large programming classes
target_learning_goals: attention, engagement and logical thinking during lessons
key_sources: van Niekerk, J.F. (2015). The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic. Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2016.09.008

article_title: Using Internet videos to learn about controversies: Evaluation and integration of multiple and multimodal documents by primary school students
citation: Salmerón, L., Sampietro, A., & Delgado, P. (2020). Using Internet videos to learn about controversies: Evaluation and integration of multiple and multimodal documents by primary school students. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103907
title: Shallowing hypothesis as an account of modality effects on integration
description: The shallowing hypothesis holds that interactions with digital media are "quick episodes driven by immediate rewards", so processing becomes superficial and constructing coherent representations of complex information is difficult. The article applies it to Internet videos, predicting that "learning from Internet videos will result in lower comprehension and integration than when reading textual pages" because students consume videos mainly for entertainment. The study's inference contrast between two texts and two videos is offered as support.
requirements: Students must have habitual, entertainment-oriented experience with the digital medium for shallow processing to be expected
constraints: The article frames the hypothesis around quick, reward-driven interactions with digital media rather than all digital use
target_learning_goals: integrated understanding of controversial socio-scientific topics from multiple documents
examples: The study compared two-text and two-video conditions with equal exposure time and found the inference advantage for texts
key_sources: Salmerón, L., Sampietro, A., & Delgado, P. (2020). Using Internet videos to learn about controversies: Evaluation and integration of multiple and multimodal documents by primary school students. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103796

article_title: Fostering inclusion in healthcare: a systematic review of collaborative teaching with individuals with disorders of intellectual development.
citation: Felix Gorny, Anika Grohmann, Mareike Müller-Cleve, Daniela Bavaresco, Saskia Wirtz, Christan Brandt, Tanja Sappok. (2026). Fostering inclusion in healthcare: a systematic review of collaborative teaching with individuals with disorders of intellectual development. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09930-0
title: Three-year qualification programme 'From sheltered workshop to university' for educational specialists with intellectual disabilities
description: A conceptual and practice-oriented guideline describing a "structured three-year qualification program featuring modules on work and education, participation, educational practice, teaching methods, and assessment" that prepares adults with intellectual disabilities and prior sheltered-workshop experience for employment as educational specialists at universities. Graduates act as experts by experience, co-design and co-deliver teaching using biographical material, work in co-teaching tandems with academic staff, and function as change agents for inclusive institutional development. Several cohorts of approximately 6–8 participants have completed the qualification at different universities.
requirements: Sustainable structural anchoring such as cooperation agreements, long-term funding, and involvement in committees
Systematic integration of theory, practice placements, and psychosocial support
constraints: The guideline is not primarily an empirical research study; it synthesizes conceptual foundations and implementation experiences
target_learners: adults with intellectual disabilities transitioning from sheltered workshops
university students taught by the qualified specialists
target_learning_goals: lived-experience perspectives on inclusion and exclusion
examples: Two included studies reported a three-year training program for co-teachers; the guideline reports associated empowerment effects such as enhanced self-efficacy, social recognition, and independent income
key_sources: Felix Gorny, Anika Grohmann, Mareike Müller-Cleve, Daniela Bavaresco, Saskia Wirtz, Christan Brandt, Tanja Sappok. (2026). article_title: Effectiveness of virtual reality in nursing education: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Liu Kai, Zhang Weiwei, Li Wei, Wang Ting, Zheng Yanxue. (2023). Effectiveness of virtual reality in nursing education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04662-x
title: Sherman and Craig's four essential components of VR as the review's defining criterion for VR-based instruction
description: The review operationalizes VR instruction using the four essential components delineated by Sherman and Craig: "virtual world, immersion, sensory feedback, interactivity". Included studies' experimental groups had to employ VR technology implementing these components to establish varying degrees of immersion through diverse VR platforms. This definition distinguishes VR interventions from non-VR simulation controls such as high-fidelity/low-fidelity and mannequin simulation.
requirements: Experimental interventions must implement virtual world, immersion, sensory feedback, and interactivity to count as VR instruction
constraints: The criterion was applied only to randomized controlled trials in nursing student populations
examples: Included interventions ranged from immersive VR (Immer VR) to VR combined with online education and flipped-classroom VR animation micro-courses
key_sources: Liu Kai, Zhang Weiwei, Li Wei, Wang Ting, Zheng Yanxue. (2023). Effectiveness of virtual reality in nursing education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04662-x

article_title: Expediency of Study of the Scientists' Biographies in Physics Course
citation: Korsun, I. (2017). Expediency of Study of the Scientists' Biographies in Physics Course. International Journal of Instruction, 10(2), 229-244. http://www.e-iji.net/dosyalar/iji_2017_2_15.pdf
title: Present scientists as real humans with drawbacks and disputes to develop learners' critical thinking
description: The article recommends against idealised portrayals of scientists. As printed, "No need to portray scientists completely devoid of drawbacks. The history of science knows a lot of disputes between scientists. These examples will develop the critical thinking of learners." It also advises avoiding superlative praise such as "the greatest scientist of Century" and instead describing the state of physics before the scientist's work and his contribution, showing that great discoveries build on many scientists' work.
requirements: Teachers should avoid expressions of excessive praise and instead situate each scientist's contribution relative to prior work by other scientists
constraints: The recommendation is grounded in the author's teaching experience and historical examples rather than in a tested comparison
target_learning_goals: realistic understanding of the nature of scientific work
examples: The article cites the Newton-Hooke dispute over the gravitational interaction law and the Röntgen-Puliui X-ray priority question as usable classroom examples
key_sources: Korsun, I. (2017). Expediency of Study of the Scientists' Biographies in Physics Course. International Journal of Instruction, 10(2), 229-244. http://www.e-iji.net/dosyalar/iji_2017_2_15.pdf

article_title: SHINE in Secondaries: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Victoria Menzies, Clare Collyer, Dimitra Kokotsaki, Catherine Hewitt, Kirsty Younger, Andy Wiggins and Carole Torgerson. (2015). SHINE in Secondaries: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: SHINE in Secondaries Saturday school programme
description: A grant-funded Saturday school transition programme run by secondary schools for underachieving Year 7 pupils, targeting literacy, numeracy, social networks, social skills and self-confidence. Schools run 25 weekly Saturday sessions (or 21 five-hour sessions in one project) for around 60 pupils divided into three classes of up to 24, with "four qualified teachers, three teaching assistants and three peer mentors all recruited and employed by the host secondary school". Schools develop their own themed curriculum following SHINE's guiding principles, supported by the 'Making it Work' handbook and medium-term plans.
requirements: Staffing of four qualified teachers, three teaching assistants and three peer mentors per project of around 60 pupils
School-developed curriculum following SHINE's guiding principles, with a termly theme and medium-term plans shared with the SHINE programme manager
constraints: Uptake was 73% of pupils assigned to the intervention, creating a fuzzy design; average attendance among accepters was 68%
Funding of £52,000 per school, around £870 per pupil per year at 60 pupils, with schools expected to co-fund from Year 4 onward
target_learners: Year 7 pupils who did not achieve Level 4 at Key Stage 2 in disadvantaged urban secondary schools
target_learning_goals: social skills and confidence during primary-secondary transition
examples: Three projects ran 25 Saturday sessions of four hours; one ran 21 sessions of five hours, all from November 2013 to June/July 2014
key_sources: Victoria Menzies, Clare Collyer, Dimitra Kokotsaki, Catherine Hewitt, Kirsty Younger, Andy Wiggins and Carole Torgerson. (2015). SHINE in Secondaries: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581429

article_title: SHINE in Secondaries: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Victoria Menzies, Clare Collyer, Dimitra Kokotsaki, Catherine Hewitt, Kirsty Younger, Andy Wiggins and Carole Torgerson. (2015). SHINE in Secondaries: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: SHINE guiding principles for a creative Saturday-school curriculum
description: SHINE specifies guiding principles that host schools use to design their own Saturday curriculum: a core focus on literacy and numeracy around a termly theme; opportunities to revisit areas of struggle and extend beyond weekday subjects; hands-on project work and enrichment applying learning to real-world contexts; curricular flexibility for trips and visits to re-engage demotivated pupils; and "an emphasis on investigative and collaborative learning and research projects which encourage problem solving and independent learning". The pattern structures a 25-week enrichment-oriented catch-up programme.
requirements: A termly theme chosen by the school linking literacy and numeracy work
Educational visits connected to the theme and a subject area, funded from a dedicated budget
Medium-term planning demonstrating how learning links between Saturdays
constraints: Schools, not SHINE, design the specific curriculum, so implementation varies by host school
target_learners: underachieving Year 7 pupils in the transition year of secondary school
examples: Projects integrated residential trips, enrichment activities or additional English and maths tutors using unspent summer-school funding
key_sources: Victoria Menzies, Clare Collyer, Dimitra Kokotsaki, Catherine Hewitt, Kirsty Younger, Andy Wiggins and Carole Torgerson. (2015). SHINE in Secondaries: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581429

article_title: The Effect of Using the Story-Mapping Technique on Developing Tenth Grade Students' Short Story Writing Skills in EFL
citation: Salem Saleh Khalaf Ibnian. (2010). The Effect of Using the Story-Mapping Technique on Developing Tenth Grade Students' Short Story Writing Skills in EFL. English Language Teaching, Vol. 3, No. 4. http://www.ccsenet.org/elt
title: Taxonomy of short story writing skills for tenth-grade EFL students
description: The article organizes short story writing ability into four skill domains validated by a jury-processed checklist: Content and Organization (availability and clarity of story elements, plot, coherent and logically sequenced content), Mechanics of Writing (punctuation, spelling, grammar), Language Use (appropriate words and accurate expressions), and Creative Abilities (fluency, flexibility, novelty, elaboration). The checklist began as a "16- skill checklist" and skills agreed upon by at least 75% of jury members were retained. This taxonomy structures both the study's scoring scale and its conclusions about where story-mapping helped.
requirements: Skills identified through literature review and jury validation, with skills agreed upon by at least 75% of jury members selected
constraints: Some proposed skills were deleted as above tenth-grade level, so the taxonomy is calibrated to tenth grade
target_learning_goals: short story writing skills including content and organization, mechanics, language use, and creative abilities
examples: The scoring scale weighted the domains as Content and Organization 30, Mechanics of Writing 15, Language Use 10, and Creative Abilities 20 out of 75 total points.
key_sources: Salem Saleh Khalaf Ibnian. (2010). The Effect of Using the Story-Mapping Technique on Developing Tenth Grade Students' Short Story Writing Skills in EFL. English Language Teaching, Vol. 3, No. 4. http://www.ccsenet.org/elt

article_title: The Effect of Using the Story-Mapping Technique on Developing Tenth Grade Students' Short Story Writing Skills in EFL
citation: Salem Saleh Khalaf Ibnian. (2010). The Effect of Using the Story-Mapping Technique on Developing Tenth Grade Students' Short Story Writing Skills in EFL. English Language Teaching, Vol. 3, No. 4. http://www.ccsenet.org/elt
title: Pre-post short story writing test with a five-level scoring scale
description: The study's measurement instrument is a pre-post short story writing test with an accompanying scoring scale, scored out of 75 across Content and Organization (30), Mechanics of Writing (15), Language Use (10), and Creative Abilities (20), each rated on a five-level scale from excellent to poor. Test reliability via Cronbach Alpha was 0.90; inter-rater reliability was 0.91 and intra-rater reliability 0.95. Test duration was set at 60 minutes, derived from the fastest and slowest students' times.
requirements: Administered to both groups before and after the treatment; scored by trained raters using the five-level scale
constraints: Validity and reliability established with jury review and a separate 25-student pilot sample, not with the study sample itself
target_learning_goals: short story writing skills in EFL
examples: The test was administered on Sep. 8th, 2009 (pre-test) and Dec. 13th, 2009 (post-test) to both groups.
key_sources: Salem Saleh Khalaf Ibnian. (2010). The Effect of Using the Story-Mapping Technique on Developing Tenth Grade Students' Short Story Writing Skills in EFL. English Language Teaching, Vol. 3, No. 4. http://www.ccsenet.org/elt

article_title: Does Project-Based Learning Enhance Iranian EFL Learners' Vocabulary Recall and Retention?
citation: Shafaei, A., & Abdul Rahim, H. (2015). Does project-based learning enhance Iranian EFL learners' vocabulary recall and retention? Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research, 3(2), 83-99. https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr
title: Replace rote, translation-based vocabulary teaching with interactive, project-based methods
description: The article argues that parrot-like repetition and translation of words does not work well and that learners need an active role in their learning. It recommends that "A conscious effort must be made to move away from the existing traditional practices to more effective, practical and useful methods, such as the PBL method", particularly in the Iranian EFL context where grammar-translation and audio-lingual approaches dominate. The principle rests on the study's finding that PBL learners recalled and retained significantly more vocabulary than conventionally taught learners.
requirements: Learners work cooperatively on authentic projects that require applying the target vocabulary
Teachers provide topics, feedback and opportunities for oral and written reporting
constraints: The authors caution that findings may not generalize to all Iranian EFL learners because participants came from one area of the country, and say the results are not conclusive
examples: The experimental group learned 30 lexical items through weekly group projects while the control group received teacher-centred translation-based instruction with textbook exercises
key_sources: Shafaei, A., & Abdul Rahim, H. (2015). Does project-based learning enhance Iranian EFL learners' vocabulary recall and retention? Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research, 3(2), 83-99. https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr

article_title: A Quasi-Experimental Study on Using Short Stories: Statistical and Inferential Analyses on the Non-English Major University Students' Speaking and Writing Achievements
citation: Jaya Nur IMAN. (2017). A QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL STUDY ON USING SHORT STORIES: STATISTICAL AND INFERENTIAL ANALYSES ON THE NON-ENGLISH MAJOR UNIVERSITY STUDENTS' SPEAKING AND WRITING ACHIEVEMENTS. International Journal of Languages' Education and Teaching, 5(1). https://doi.org/10.18298/ijlet.1719
title: Short-stories lesson sequence: group reading, individual oral summary, then written summary paragraphs
description: A lesson-level instructional pattern in which learners first read a short story together, then produce an oral summary, then a written one. The article's procedure was that "the researcher asked the students to read the short story silently and loudly with their peers in a group", after which students made an individual oral summary in front of the class and wrote three to four paragraphs. It was implemented in the experimental group as the English teaching activity, drawing on stories from Intermediate Stories for Reproduction 1.
requirements: Stories must be selected appropriate to students' level of language proficiency, which the article says lets instructors avoid "frustration reading"
constraints: The article's procedure section states the experiment occurred in 12 teaching sessions of 90 minutes, while the abstract states the treatment was given for 14 meetings; the article does not reconcile this discrepancy
examples: The experimental group read short stories with peers, gave individual oral summaries in front of the class, and wrote out three to four paragraphs from the story read

article_title: Using Rubrics as an Instructional Tool in EFL Writing Courses
citation: Turgut, F., & Kayaoğlu, M. N. (2015). Using rubrics as an instructional tool in EFL writing courses. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 11(1), 47-58. http://www.jlls.org
title: Share and teach assessment criteria with students rather than keeping grading criteria private
description: The article argues teachers who keep their own criteria for assessment to themselves create inconsistent assessment and student-teacher disputes over grades. Sharing rubrics and involving students in assessment is presented as making students part of the assessment process and improving writing, since "students primarily benefit because they will write better essays when they understand the cr iteria their teachers will use to evaluate their writing".
requirements: Clear criteria for assessing writing and student involvement in the assessment process, per the article's four characteristics of effective assessment
constraints: The article notes rubric use did not liberate students from the teacher's authority, and teachers remained students' primary audience
target_learners: EFL university students in writing courses
target_learning_goals: writing performance and understanding the qualities of good writing
examples: The experimental group was guided in using the rubric while writing two essay types, while the control group wrote the same essay types without the rubric

article_title: Efficacy of an Electronic Editing Strategy with College Students with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities
citation: Suzanne Woods-Groves, Youjia Hua, Jeremy W. Ford, Katelyn M. Neil. (2017). Efficacy of an Electronic Editing Strategy with College Students with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities. Education and Training in Autism and Developmental Disabilities, 52(4), 422-436. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=EDIT+Strategy+editing+college+students+intellectual+developmental+disabilities
title: Pair a shortened strategy intervention with an expanded dependent measure to detect improvement efficiently
description: The article recommends determining the most efficient intervention design by shortening instruction while extending the outcome measure. "These findings support the use of a shorter intervention (i.e., 11 vs. 16 sessions) coupled with the revised dependent measure." In this study the intervention was reduced from 16 to 11 sessions (8.25 vs. 13.3 hours) while the pre-/posttest prompts were expanded from 25 to 30 errors, and students still improved on more error types than in the prior 16-session study.
requirements: Dependent measure with enough error instances to avoid a ceiling effect and expand the measurable range of performance
Explicit strategy instruction with mastery criterion maintained despite fewer sessions
constraints: The shortened intervention still required 8.25 hours and 11 sessions; the authors call for further investigation of even shorter intervention times
target_learners: postsecondary students with intellectual and developmental disabilities
examples: The study reduced sessions from 16 to 11 by removing lessons on spell-check review and guided practice with all steps, while expanding prompts from 25 to 30 errors
key_sources: Suzanne Woods-Groves, Youjia Hua, Jeremy W. Ford, Katelyn M. Neil. (2017). Efficacy of an Electronic Editing Strategy with College Students with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities. Education and Training in Autism and Developmental Disabilities, 52(4), 422-436. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1160277

article_title: Alleviating Mathematics Anxiety of Elementary School Students: A Situated Perspective
citation: Sharma, Y. (2016). Alleviating mathematics anxiety of elementary school students: A situated perspective. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 2(2), 509-517. https://www.ijres.net
title: Mathematics Anxiety Scale by Sharma and Sansanwal (2011)
description: A 44-item self-report measure of mathematics anxiety covering cognitive and affective dimensions, used as both pretest and posttest in this study. The article reports: "The test -retest reliability and split-half reliability coefficients were reported as .80 and .82 respectively" and a criterion validity of –.74 against a mathematics achievement test. Positive and negative items (22 each) are scored 1–3 with no time limit, generally taking about 25 minutes.
requirements: Administered identically at pretest and posttest to both groups for ANCOVA covariate use
constraints: Designed for school children; used here with grade VII students in English-medium schools
target_learners: school students (grade VII in this study)
target_learning_goals: measuring mathematics anxiety as an outcome of instruction
examples: Served as the dependent measure in the 2×2 ANCOVA, with pretest scores as the covariate
key_sources: Sharma, Y. (2016). Alleviating mathematics anxiety of elementary school students: A situated perspective. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 2(2), 509-517. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1110268

article_title: The Effectiveness of Learning Geography Using Computer-Based Games
citation: Jerry Prell, William R. Nelson, and John Foshay. (2012). The Effectiveness of Learning Geography Using Computer-based Games. Journal of Special Education Apprenticeship, Vol. 1, No. 2. https://sheppardsoftware.com/USA_Geography/USA_G2_double2.html
title: Sheppardsoftware.com States Level 3 and States Level 6 computer-based map games
description: Two free online U.S.A. map games used as the intervention and assessment tools in the study. "States Level 3 required players to drag each of the 50 states to the correct location and drop it there, like putting together pieces of a puzzle." States Level 6 had the same requirements but states disappear once placed correctly, so the game becomes progressively more difficult as visual cues decrease. Students played three consecutive trials per day for three days, recording and saving scores.
requirements: A computer lab with access to the Sheppardsoftware.com U.S.A. Games pages and directions with an embedded hyperlink to the correct game
constraints: The article notes the games are on a publicly available website which students could have accessed from home, a stated history-effect risk
target_learners: seventh-grade middle school social studies students, including students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: identifying the names, shapes, and locations of the 50 U.S. states on a map
examples: Students played 3 consecutive trials per day for 3 days, recording and saving scores in network folders after each session
key_sources: Jerry Prell, William R. Nelson, and John Foshay. (2012). The Effectiveness of Learning Geography Using Computer-based Games. Journal of Special Education Apprenticeship, Vol. 1, No. 2. https://sheppardsoftware.com/USA_Geography/USA_G2_double2.html

article_title: The Application of Humorous Song in EFL Classrooms and Its Effects on Listening Comprehension
citation: Marzieh Rafiee, Zohre Kassaian, Hossein Vahid Dastjerdi. (2010). The Application of Humorous Song in EFL Classrooms and Its Effects on Listening Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 3(4). http://www.ccsenet.org/elt
title: Shel Silverstein humorous songs as listening-treatment material
description: The study's treatment material was a set of humorous songs: "the poems written and sung by Shel Silverstein were chosen". Silverstein (1930-1999) was an American poet, singer-songwriter and children's author whose quirky style is described as laid-back and conversational, occasionally employing fancy and jokes. One song, "SICK", is reproduced in Appendix 3 as an example of the material learners heard.
requirements: Songs must be humorous and suited to relaxed listening without follow-up questions
constraints: The authors state the materials should be adapted to non-native learners, in higher quality sound and slower text reading pace
target_learning_goals: listening comprehension through aural exposure to humorous songs
examples: The poem-song "SICK", about a child listing imaginary ailments to avoid school, was among the songs played in the treatment sessions.

article_title: Can a "Shouting" Digital Game Help Learners Develop Oral Fluency in a Second Language?
citation: Grimshaw, J., Cardoso, W., & Waddington, D. (2016). Can a ‘shouting’ digital game help learners develop oral fluency in a second language?. In S. Papadima-Sophocleous, L. Bradley & S. Thouësny (Eds), CALL communities and culture – short papers from EUROCALL 2016 (pp. 172-177). Research-publishing.net. https://doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2016.eurocall2016.557
title: Use time-sensitive collaborative mobile games as warm-up activities to encourage fluency development in a non-threatening environment
description: The article proposes using Spaceteam ESL as a fluency development activity because it fulfils Nation and Newton's (2008) requirements: it "encourages players to speed up the use of language items" and to process a large amount of input efficiently. It also offers a pre-prepared activity "requiring little preparation from the classroom teacher" and may reduce anxiety and increase willingness to communicate.
requirements: Activities must encourage speeding up the use of previously acquired language items and processing large amounts of input, per Nation and Newton (2008)
constraints: The study found no significant difference between groups; the authors state further research under more controllable conditions and a longer treatment period is needed
examples: The treatment group played Spaceteam ESL for 15 minutes as a warm-up in class for six weeks while the control group did info gap, story retelling, and other interactive activities

article_title: Teacher and Student Based Instructions on Probability Achievement Outcomes and Attitudes of Secondary School Students in Bungoma North, Kenya
citation: Joseph W. Pale. (2016). Teacher and Student Based Instructions on Probability Achievement Outcomes and Attitudes of Secondary School Students in Bungoma North, Kenya. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.24. https://www.iiste.org
title: Mathematics teachers should shift from teacher-based to student-based teaching methods and help students make sense of mathematics rather than memorise formulas
description: Based on the study's findings, the author recommends that mathematics teachers recognise the benefits of student-based learning and change their practice accordingly. The article concludes that "teachers who teach mathematics need to be aware of the benefits and importance of student based learni ng and thus change the practice of teacher- based teaching  methods to student based teaching methods." It further urges teachers to provide learning opportunities in which students experience the excitement of making sense of mathematics instead of memorising formulas and rules, and to help students see connections between school mathematics and fields such as engineering, science and technology.
requirements: Teachers must establish participation structures, monitor and adjust group arrangements, and value student contributions and explanations
constraints: The study was conducted in five secondary schools in Bungoma North district, so the author notes it may not be possible to generalise the results to a larger population
examples: The article recommends that teachers "provide students with learning opportunities in which they experience the excitement that comes from making sense of mathematics instead of memorizing formulas and rules", based on the finding that students viewed probability as important but lacked perseverance

article_title: Valuing a More Rigorous Review of Formative Assessment's Effectiveness
citation: Apthorp, H., Klute, M., Petrites, T., Harlacher, J., & Reale, M. (2016). Valuing a more rigorous review of formative assessment's effectiveness. SREE Spring 2016 Conference Proposal. https://www.relcentral.org/news-and-events/the-essence-of-formative-assessment-creating-a-common-understanding-of-the-formative-assessment-process/
title: Define formative assessment as short-cycle evidence gathering during instruction to adjust learning, distinguishing it from summative data use
description: The review defines formative assessment as "a process that engages teachers and students during instruction in continuous, systematic evidence gathering to improve student learning", focusing on cycles occurring within minutes, days, or weeks. The article argues the utility of the shorter cycle is in adjusting instruction, while the utility of the longer cycle is in adjusting curriculum, so summative testing information can be used formatively but the review's scope is the short or medium cycle.
requirements: The evidence-gathering and interpreting cycle must occur during instruction within a short or medium period of time (minutes, days, or weeks)
constraints: The review excludes uses of end-of-course, end-of-grade, or other summative testing data as its focus, though such information can be used formatively at any time
target_learners: students in grades 1-6, including regular education students and students with learning disabilities, emotional disturbance, and/or intellectual disabilities
target_learning_goals: improving student academic achievement through adjusted instruction
examples: The review applies this definition to classify interventions across mathematics, reading, writing, science, technology and engineering, music and physical education

article_title: The Formation of Learners' Motivation to Study Physics in Terms of Sustainable Development of Education in Ukraine
citation: Igor Korsun. (2017). The Formation of Learnersí Motivation to Study Physics in Terms of Sustainable Development of Education in Ukraine. Journal of Teacher Education for Sustainability, vol. 19, no. 1, pp. 117ñ128. https://doi.org/10.1515/jtes-2017-0008
title: Short-term and long-term objectives of interest formation in physics
description: The article distinguishes two objectives of the formation of learners' motivation to study physics: "Its short-term objective was the formation of learners' interest in physics as a school subject. Its long-term objective was the formation of learners' interest in physics as a science." The short-term objective is served by situational interest created through active means and methods in lessons, while the long-term objective corresponds to the transition toward individual interest. Achieving this should contribute to professional self-determination of learners.
requirements: Sustained use of active means of training and active learning methods over time
target_learners: secondary school learners aged 15ñ17 studying physics
target_learning_goals: interest in physics as a school subject and as a science, and professional self-determination

article_title: Improving EFL Learners' Writing through Enhanced Extensive Reading
citation: Mermelstein, A. D. (2015). Improving EFL learners’ writing through enhanced extensive reading. Reading in a Foreign Language, 27(2), 182–198. http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl
title: Keep in-class extensive reading short (about 15–20 minutes) and sustain it across a full year, supported by out-of-class reading
description: The article's enhanced ER design rests on five conditions: a large variety of reading materials, placing learners at their optimal reading levels (95 percent vocabulary understanding), a longer balanced duration across the school year, minimizing daily in-class ER to 15–20 minutes, and placing less accountability on learners. The author argues this makes ER feasible for teachers who cannot devote large class periods to reading. The study reports that "only approximately 15 minutes of ER needs to take place in the classroom if it is supported by outside reading" to produce significant learning results.
requirements: A large variety of level-appropriate reading materials must be available for learners to select from
Learners must be placed in their optimal reading levels, operationalized in the study as 95 percent understanding of the text level vocabulary
Learners must continue reading outside class, with the study expecting a minimum of three pages per day
constraints: The author states there is not a one size fits all method, and the comparison with prior studies could not directly compare total out-of-class reading time because other studies did not report it
target_learners: University EFL learners in mixed-ability classes
target_learning_goals: EFL writing skills: content, organization, vocabulary, language use, mechanics, and fluency
examples: The treatment group read in class once per week as a sustained silent reading activity of on average 15 to 20 minutes, continued graded reader reading at home with a minimum of three pages per day, and were not required to write reports about their books
key_sources: Mermelstein, A. D. (2015). Improving EFL learners’ writing through enhanced extensive reading. Reading in a Foreign Language, 27(2), 182–198. http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl

article_title: A Sharing Mind Map-Oriented Approach to Enhance Collaborative Mobile Learning with Digital Archiving Systems
citation: Chang, Chiu, and Huang. (2018). A Sharing Mind Map-oriented Approach to Enhance Collaborative Mobile Learning With Digital Archiving Systems. International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning, 19(1). https://irrodl.org
title: Sharing mind map (SMM) mobile learning system integrated with digital archiving
description: A mobile collaborative learning system combining mind maps with digital archive resources, built with HTML and JavaScript, XML data files, and a PHP framework so it runs on different platforms and mobile devices. It includes teacher-side modules (mind map theme setting, pre-and-post test score management, digital archive information management) and student-side modules for learning mind maps, tests, a system questionnaire, and a Facebook-based community sharing module. The system "recommended mind maps with similar knowledge structures for learners to observe" so they could modify their own maps, and keywords entered by students automatically brought up relevant digital archive maps.
requirements: Teacher establishes mind map themes, uploads relevant digital archive materials, and sets pre-and-post test questions in the server before activities
constraints: Some introduced archive resources had low authenticity, missing or unreliable collections, unclear photo provenance, and the interface lacked user instructions or tips
target_learning_goals: local history and social studies knowledge construction
examples: Students used the theme of Danshui, viewing scenes from Japanese colonial times and the present, completing mind maps with keywords, site addresses, and uploaded pictures

article_title: A Sharing Mind Map-Oriented Approach to Enhance Collaborative Mobile Learning with Digital Archiving Systems

description: The article recommends that teachers consider students' proficiency when selecting video length, noting that "videos shorter than five minutes are usually enough for students who learn a foreign language" and that short clips (1-5 words) yielded higher listening success than long clips (6-20 words) among low-medium proficiency learners.

article_title: The Art of Teaching Science in Secondary Schools: A Meta Analysis
citation: Sharifah Sariah Syed Hassan, Ahmad Abdullahi Ibrahim. (2018). The Art of Teaching Science in Secondary Schools: A Meta Analysis. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(1).
title: Science teachers should shift from teacher-centred to student-centred instruction to improve learning and motivation
description: The review finds science teachers are moving away from teacher-centred methods, in which the teacher dominates learning activities, toward student-centred methods offering opportunities to discover scientific facts themselves. It reports "they are making effort to shift their instruction from teacher centred to student centred method which offers more opportunities for students to discover scientific facts and mathematic solutions by themselves". Student-centred approaches such as problem-based, cooperative and discovery learning were associated with better performance and motivation in the reviewed studies.
requirements: Selection of methods depends on lesson objectives, students' characteristics, subject nature, student population and teacher competency
constraints: One reviewed PBL study found the control group showed higher interest in mathematics than the PBL group
examples: Abdullah, Tarmizi and Abu (2010) found PBL students obtained higher scores and teamwork; Vlassi and Karaliota (2012) found guided inquiry superior to traditional teaching for the structure of matter

title: Show teachers evidence of student achievement to convince them to change their practices
description: This study reinforces the importance of including evidence of student achievement in any models supporting teacher change in practice. Teacher educators should emphasize showing evidence of students' achievement in order to convince teachers to change their practices. Convincing teachers in terms of student learning outcomes may then initiate a change in their beliefs about reform and IBI.
requirements: Periodic tests might allow teachers to evaluate how much their changes in instructional practices contribute to their students' academic achievement.

examples: During the final follow-up meeting, participating teachers had a chance to view students' progress from fall to the spring semester.

article_title: An Empirical Study on Alleviating Career English Writing Anxiety through Cooperative Learning in a Chinese Polytechnic Institute
citation: Jiang, D. (2016). An Empirical Study on Alleviating Career English Writing Anxiety through Cooperative Learning in a Chinese Polytechnic Institute. International Journal of Higher Education, 5(1), 173. https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v5n1p173
title: Use shared group rewards and structured role rotation to make cooperative writing anxiety-reducing
description: The article's cooperative writing model assigns four rotating roles across planning, drafting, revising, and editing steps, with the final draft scored as group credit. The "shared risks, joint rewards" principle meant "if all the members of one group scored 10 on the writi ng assignment, each could receive 10 for their performance score." This design removes individual humiliation while keeping every member accountable for at least one step each assignment.
requirements: Heterogeneous groups of four mixing English levels, learning styles, and personalities
Group credit counts toward individual performance scores (70% of final score in this study)
Each member is responsible for at least one of the four writing steps per assignment
constraints: Requires about one month of preparation so students know each other's abilities before grouping
Structured guidelines for planning and editing are needed, since lack of structure is a main reason cooperative writing fails to improve writing
target_learning_goals: reduction of foreign language writing anxiety
examples: Seven career-English assignments (meeting notice, customer complaint, memo) of about 100 words each, with roles rotating so each member led each step at least once

citation: Yu Yang, Luoye Fangxin, You Danhui, Xu Zhenhong, Liu Yuping, Wu Li, Deng Qian, Ning Yanting, Liu Liqiong. (2026). Heterogeneity and associated factors of palliative care core competency among oncology nurses: a latent profile analysis. PeerJ. https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.21645
title: Shared decision-making and symptom management theories as a conceptual framework for multidimensional palliative care competency
description: The article frames palliative care core competency as a multidimensional construct guided by two theoretical perspectives: shared decision-making, which "emphasizes communication, value clarification and patient participation in preference-sensitive care decisions closely related to ethical care competency", and symptom management frameworks, which focus on "symptom assessment, intervention, and outcome evaluation", related to clinical practice competence and psychological adjustment. Together these provide the conceptual basis for treating competency as multidimensional rather than a single overall skill, and they guided the person-centered LPA of oncology nurses.
requirements: Requires multidimensional assessment covering ethical care, clinical practice, and psychological self-adjustment dimensions
constraints: The article notes few studies have used these frameworks to guide person-centered analyses of competency heterogeneity
examples: The study used the three competency dimensions derived from these theories as continuous indicators in the latent profile analysis.

description: The article recommends structuring curriculum development as a collaborative effort between the AMS team and the nursing department, using a shared governance model that ensures shared decision-making, accountability, and ownership. Task forces comprising nurse experts from middle-level nursing leadership and nurse educators ensured "the relevance and agreement of the nursing department at all stages of curriculum development." Formation of a task force with nurse experts and nurse educators representing different specialties

examples: The nursing curriculum development and content review task force held seven meetings led by the AMS nurse and AMS clinical pharmacist with participation of nurse experts

title: Shared Mental Model theory as an account of cohort differences in PBL network structure
description: The article invokes Shared Mental Model (SMM) theory to explain why Year 2 PBL networks were more cohesive than Year 1 networks. SMM proposes that "understanding how members work towards a common goal, within an environment characterised by the knowledge structure of each team member, builds the foundation of effective teamwork". Early in PBL, students depend on a few peers to organise ideas, yielding higher betweenness and modularity; with experience, triadic closure increases and reliance on brokers falls, as observed in Year 2.
requirements: Repeated PBL experience through which students negotiate and share strategies, allowing shared expectations and team knowledge structures to form.
constraints: The article presents SMM as an interpretive account of the observed cross-sectional cohort differences, not as a tested mechanism in this study.
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students in problem-based learning cohorts
examples: The authors read the Year 2 pattern of higher transitivity and reduced reliance on broker roles as closely reflecting SMM.

This lets the trial compare "the added value of post-lecture training formats", though it means the independent effect of each stand-alone modality cannot be isolated.

Standardized modality-specific duration across groups

Better suited to comparing post-lecture formats than isolating stand-alone modality effects

It was derived through a three-round Delphi process in which "All final six items met the consensus criteria (stability ≤0.2, convergence ≤0.5, agreed ≥70%)". citation: Sohail Fadieleh A, Iqbal Marium, Malik Marib Ghulam Rasool, Saeed Sana. (2025). Perspectives of faculty, students and patients on clinical skills teaching in undergraduate medical education in Pakistan: a qualitative study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2025-103139
title: The ship metaphor framework for clinical skills education
description: The article develops a metaphorical organising framework in which clinical skills education is pictured as "a ship's journey, where the student is the ship, navigating through stormy seas representing the challenges." Six metaphors structure the findings: the safety harness (simulation), the underwater life (bedside learning), the stormy seas (barriers), the ship (the student), the engine room tools (teaching modalities) and the guiding compass (faculty mentorship). Metaphors served as analytic tools condensing codes from faculty, student and patient groups into shared conceptual frames for triangulation. The framework underpins the authors' cross-cutting tensions of safety versus authenticity, standardisation versus variability, and mentorship versus service pressure.
requirements: Multi-stakeholder qualitative data so that metaphors can condense codes from diverse participant groups into shared frames
constraints: Developed and validated only at a single private medical college and teaching hospital in Pakistan, limiting transfer to other institutional or regional contexts
examples: Table 1 maps each metaphor (safety harness, underwater life, stormy seas, ship, engine room tools, guiding compass) to its meaning in clinical education

title: Summative assessment effectiveness requires transparency of assessment language so students are assessed on knowledge rather than on aligning with educators' interpretations
description: The article's central design principle is that high-stakes assessments communicate processing demands through action verbs and collocated words whose meanings must be shared: "assessment effectiveness must encompass transparency of language, so students are assessed on their knowledge rather than their ability to align with educators' interpretation(s)". Because verbs carry discipline-specific nuances, departments should build consensus definitions and distribute them as a shared language of assessment to staff and students.

constraints: The article states students' perspectives were beyond the study's scope and that generalizability to other assessment formats, such as MCQs, and to other institutions remains unclear.

target_learning_goals: Correctly interpreting the processing demands of summative exam questions
Demonstrating the intended level of cognitive complexity in constructed-response answers
examples: The article reports that "the consensus meanings for action verbs and collocated words provide a resource which can be distributed to staff and students, so that there is a shared language of assessment within our department".

title: Moderated mediation model: attention as mediator and parental usage duration as moderator
description: The article proposes and tests a moderated mediation model in which elementary students' short video usage lowers academic performance both directly and indirectly through reduced attention, with parental short video usage duration moderating the usage-to-attention path. title: Arrange shadowing and simulation training before redeploying junior doctors to critical care
description: This principle holds that senior clinicians and managers should listen carefully to redeployed doctors' concerns and, where operationally possible, arrange shadowing and simulation training before redeployment to critical care.
